name: SN2026ahvu
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of nearby SN 1a SN 2026ahvu
abstract: SN 2026ahvu is a Young Type Ia Supernova in NGC 1433 (9 Mpc). To put this in perspective, SN 2014J was at 3 Mpc and SN 2025rbs was at 13 Mpc (non-detection in NuSTAR 40-ks observation). This makes SN 2026ahvu the closest Type Ia supernova since SN 2014J. It is currently in the rising phase (priv comm., Jacobson-Galan) where the first spectroscopic observation occurring only a day after the last non-detection. Expectation are that optical peak emission will be in a week or two. Early hard X-rays will be associated with down-scattered 56Ni emission in the supernova ejecta.

name: 1E1048d1m5937
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of the magnetar 1E 1048.1-5937
abstract: 1E 1048.1-5937 is a uniquely valuable magnetar for testing whether magnetar activity recurs on a preferred timescale. Since the late 1990s, the source has shown major radiative/torque events separated by roughly five years. Its most recent outburst occurred in July 2022, ~5 yr after the previous event, placing the next expected active epoch in 2027. Our long-term flux and spin-down history highlights this remarkable recurrent behavior (please see light curve in goole drive and Archibald et al. 2020). We request 8x5 ks NuSTAR observations, spaced every three weeks through 31 January 2027, to test whether this apparent ~5 yr cycle persists and to identify the onset of renewed activity. This cadence will establish the current pre-outburst baseline while constraining the onset time of any new event to within ~3 weeks. If activity is detected, we will trigger IXPE to obtain a polarization view of this unusual magnetar; after January, we hope to continue the campaign through a joint IXPE+NuSTAR GO proposal. These short visits are sufficient. At the current 3-79 keV count rate of 0.2 counts s-1 (FPMA+FPMB), 5 ks constrains the 3-10 keV absorption-corrected flux to (4.0 +/- 0.4)x10-12 erg s-1 cm-2 (<10%) and detects the pulse at >10sigma. This DDT request is driven by an unexpected loss of monitoring capability. With Swift/XRT science operations suspended and NICER unavailable, NuSTAR is presently the only practical facility able to provide the repeated sensitive timing and flux measurements required for this experiment. Unfortunately, this situation could not have been anticipated in the regular NuSTAR GO program, because the GO deadline preceded the announcement that Swift would cease science operations. Missing this interval would create a critical gap in a >20-year experiment.

name: NGC5907_ULX1
title: NuSTAR DDT snapshot observation of NGC 5907 ULX1
abstract: NGC5907 ULX1 is the most luminous of the known ULX pulsars, reaching X-ray luminosities of Lx ~ 1e41 erg/s and thus revealing an extreme accretion regime that extends up to ~500x Eddington. Such extreme accretion may be required to rapidly grow supermassive black holes in the early Universe, so local examples of this accretion regime are particularly valuable, and important to understand. In NuSTAR cycle 12 we were awarded a pair of deep, coordinated XMM+NuSTAR observations of NGC5907 ULX1 with the primary scientific aim of tracking the long-term evolution of the neutron star spin. However, the first of these (taken in August) found the source in a low-flux state, rendering spin-period measurements impossible, and so we suspended the second until ULX1 had recovered its flux to a suitable level. The next XMM visibility window for NGC5907 ULX1 is opening again soon, potentially offering an opportunity to execute our outstanding XMM+NuSTAR observation, assuming ULX1 is showing a sustained recovery. In order to confirm whether this is indeed the case, or whether the XRT data were showing another of these false dawn events, we are proposing a short, confirmatory NuSTAR snapshot within the next ~week. A detection of ULX1 in this short observation would clearly indicate it is exhibiting a sustained return to activity, allowing us to re-schedule our XMM+NuSTAR observation soon after this latest turn-on.

name: 4Cp49d22
title: Extragalactic Surveys
abstract: The baseline NuSTAR extragalactic survey is comprised of three components: one deg^2 of the COSMOS field (50ks per position), 0.3 deg^2 of the ECDFS (200ks per position), and a ~3 deg^2 shallow survey (5ks per position), achieved by targeting 100 Swift-BAT identified AGNs.  Models predict that NuSTAR will detect ~200 AGNs in the COSMOS+E-CDF-S surveys and ~19 Compton-thick AGNs. The shallow survey will deliver a sample of serendipitous detection of AGNs in the NuSTAR field of view.

name: XTE_J1810m189
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of XTE J1810-189
abstract: Discovered in 2008, XTE J1810-189 is a transient neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary that had subsequent outbursts in 2012-2013, 2020, and 2023, and renewed activity in 2026 (ATel #18101). Varun et al. (2025, ApJ, 995, 153) reported a candidate thermonuclear burst oscillation at 458.92 Hz, with a trials-corrected significance of 3.14 sigma. Although this signal requires confirmation, it provides a physically motivated frequency range for a targeted search for accretion-powered pulsations. Detecting persistent or intermittent pulsations near this frequency would test the proposed spin identification and provide evidence for magnetically channelled accretion. Their energy dependence would help identify which spectral components carry the rotational modulation, connecting the coherent signal to the processes producing the X-ray continuum. A non-detection would instead constrain the pulsed fraction during the observed accretion state. NuSTAR spectroscopy would address an important limitation of previous soft X-ray observations. In the NICER study of Manca et al. (2023, MNRAS, 526, 1154), the Comptonizing electron temperature could not be constrained and was fixed at 30 keV. The reported Fe-K emission also motivates a search for broadband reflection signatures. Measuring or constraining the high-energy rollover would constrain the Comptonizing plasma's properties, while jointly modelling the continuum and any reflection would probe its geometry and interaction with the accretion disc. The ongoing outburst provides an opportunity to combine these spectral diagnostics with a targeted test of the candidate spin frequency. The spectral investigation offers an independent scientific outcome even if pulsations are not detected, while a detection would enable a direct comparison between the pulsed emission and the broadband spectrum.

name: NGC_7213
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of NGC 7213
abstract: NGC 7213 is a nearby bright low-luminosity AGN. The source shows a peculiar long-term behavior: the Einstein Observatory registered a flux of the order of ~6E-11 cgs in the 1980's. Since then the source has been observed in a continuous decay, which hinted at a possible slowly decaying TDE. An eROSITA-DR1 observation taken in 2020 at a flux of 1E-11 cgs confirmed this slow-decay behavior. The expected flux according to the long-term decay was ~8E-12 cgs. However, more recent Swift observations in 2024 revealed that the source is ~8 times brighter than expected, reaching a flux of 5.8E-11 cgs, which is close to the historical maximum flux registered by the Einstein Observatory. A similar activity has been seen across the whole electromagnetic range from radio to IR to optical up to the X-rays. Following this high-flux observation, we monitored the source for more than a year with Swift/XRT and NICER (NuSTAR+XRISM+XMM observations were taken in late 2024). The monitoring allowed us to catch the source a few more times at very high flux a few days after the first observation. After this, the source flux keeps varying on a timescale of a few days while it is still in a high flux state (average 2-10 keV flux of 4.5e-11 cgs). A decline in the flux may be expected in the coming months, if a similar pattern to the 1980's activity repeats. Our monitoring with ATCA, LBA, and GMRT showed that the source's flux has increased in the radio band, in fashion with the X-ray flux increase. However, recent LBA observations showed that the radio flux is decreasing, which may also suggest a potential decrease in the X-ray flux. Given the orbit decay of Swift (which is limiting their science observations), and the paused observations of NICER, NuSTAR is the only functioning X-ray observatory that is capable of providing a monitoring of the X-ray flux of the source. We request 4x5-ks observations with a ~monthly cadence in the period of September 19 - December 13, 2026.

name: EP260507b
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of EP260507b
abstract: We request a new NuSTAR DDT observation of EP260507b, a jetted tidal disruption event (TDE) candidate that is detected in X-ray, optical and radio bands. In the past few months, we have carried out multi-wavelength follow-up observations and we now have strong evidences that support its jetted TDE origin: 1. X-ray evolution. The flux and spectral index evolution resembles those of previously reported jetted TDEs. 2. The NuSTAR confirmation. Our previously requested NuSTAR observation (3-79 keV) accompanied with EP/FXT observation (0.3-10.0 keV) on 2026 June 16 ruled out a simple power-law (PL, #2/dof = 90.58/45) or PL+blackbody profile (90.58/43) and favored a broken PL (49.66/43). We underline that NuSTAR observation plays a key role in excluding PL since the FXT collected too few photons in 3.0-10.0 keV to exclude that. 3. Multi-wavelength counterpart and spectral energy distribution (SED): - SOAR (i-band) and SVOM/VT (VT_B/R band) precisely confirm the position of a faint optical counterpart. - MeerKAT radio observation confirm the radio counterpart at the same position (0.5" uncertainty for both counterparts). - The June 16-19 (+40-43 d) X-ray+radio SED resembles those of jetted TDEs: Swift J164449.3+573451, Swift J2058.4+0516, and AT2022cmc. The July 22 - August 10 (+75-97 d) X-ray+optical+radio SED is strikingly similar in shape to that of AT2022cmc. Recent radio observation on August 26 revealed a break at ~3 GHz in the SED, which is not displayed in any of the previous observations. Our immediate objective is to observe if the hard X-ray spectral shape has evolved following this significant evolution. If a NuSTAR DDT observation is approved, we will trigger MeerKAT, ATCA, EP/FXT & SVOM/VT optical observations and try to perform them simultaneously. This coordinated campaign will allow us to test whether the new radio spectral break is linked to an intrinsic change in the jet and to better constrain the physical mechanism driving the SED evolution.

name: SS_433
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of SS 433 coordinated with GTC/HiPERCAM
abstract: SS 433 is the only persistent Galactic super-Eddington accretor for which deep eclipses and a well-constrained precessing geometry provide a direct spatial filter on the inner accretion flow. We request two NuSTAR observations simultaneous with the two eclipse-egress visits already approved with GTC/HiPERCAM (CATESP-2026B-49). The primary experiment is eclipse-resolved optical/X-ray timing: we will measure how the detrended optical/X-ray cross-correlation evolves as the companion progressively uncovers the inner flow and jet/wind-launching region. NuSTAR uniquely provides the hard-X-ray sensitivity required during the fixed GTC windows, enabling simultaneous 3-10 and 10-30 keV light curves to test whether correlated variability changes in amplitude, lag, or sign with eclipse phase and energy. Optical/X-ray correlations and ~100-s lag structure have already been detected in SS 433; the eclipse adds the missing spatial discrimination. Archival NuSTAR data demonstrate feasibility. In the conservative eclipse benchmark ObsID 31102002004, a 30" aperture contains ~5.5e4 net counts in 3-10 keV and ~1.2e4 in 10-30 keV. Simulations show that even 3 ks yields ~1600 net 10-30 keV counts (S/N~40), recovering hard-band flux and hardness to ~3%. Sliding a 2-h window across the real GTIs gives 3.1-4.7 ks simultaneous exposure (median ~4.1 ks). The eclipse geometry makes SS 433 a benchmark for super-Eddington accretion relevant to ULXs, TDEs, and rapidly growing black holes, where orientation and outflows reshape the observed emission. CATESP-2026B-49 was submitted and awarded only after the deadline of the applicable NuSTAR GO cycle. Thus no approved optical program or actionable simultaneous opportunity existed at the GO deadline. Once GTC time was secured, that NuSTAR GO cycle had closed; DDT is therefore the only mechanism for simultaneous coverage of these time-critical observations.

name: XTE_J1637m498
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of XTE J1637-498
abstract: XTE J1637-498 was discovered by RXTE/PCA in 2008 during Galactic bulge/ridge scans ( #1699). A later analysis found detections on Aug 25.5 Aug 29.3 Sep 1.4 and Sep 5.1 (2008) with 2-10 keV fluxes of 2.5, 3.9, 2.6 and 1.8 mCrab. No pulsations, bursts or high-frequency QPOs were seen. Although a tentative ~0.2 Hz QPO was mentioned. Because limited pointed observations were made the spectrum could not be measured and the nature of the source remained unknown. No X-ray monitoring took place for the 18 years. On 2026-08-31, SRG/ART-XC noticed an outburst at the same position (ATel #18023) measuring 4.5(+-0.2)x10^-11 erg/cm2/s in the 4-12 keV band. It translates to a luminosity of about 4x10^35 erg/s assuming a distance of 8 kpc. This observation confirms that XTE J1637-498 has become active again after an 18-year silence with no monitoring in between. It would have been impossible to submit this as a GO proposal because with only two known episodes that are 18 years apart and no clear pattern. There is no solid reason to expect a future outburst. The recent activity was discovered by chance during a Galactic-plane scan than by scheduled periastron-timed monitoring. We are asking for observations with NuSTAR (3-79 keV) and XMM-Newton (0.2-12 keV with a request in parallel) to obtain the first detailed broadband spectrum of XTE J1637-498 since it was first discovered. XMM-Newton will help measure the absorption along the line of sight while NuSTAR will provide a clear view of the high-energy continuum. Together these data will allow us to make a classification of XTE J1637-498 and to look for bursts, pulsations or the tentative 2008 QPO. Any of these findings would finally answer the question about the type of accretor, in XTE J1637-498. Since the 2008 event was already fading around day 11 and the current outburst was only detected 10 days ago it is important to observe XTE J1637-498 soon as possible.

name: PNV_J19450648p1822422
title: TRACING SHOCK DEVELOPMENT IN A NOVA
abstract: We propose 3x50ks ToO observations of a new bright ($V<7.5$) nova likely to be detected in gamma-rays. The observations will trace the development of shocks within the nova ejecta, constrain the non-thermal particle acceleration and gamma-ray production mechanisms. We will put an upper limit on the particle acceleration efficiency by comparing thermal X-ray and optical to GeV luminosity and search for predicted non-thermal X-rays. Understanding nova shocks is relevant for other shock-powered transients: interacting supernovae, tidal disruption events, stellar mergers. NuSTAR is the only instrument capable of detecting hard X-rays from novae simultaneously with the GeV emission, making it critical to utilize this capability while Fermi continues operations.
subject_category: Proposed ToOs and Directors Discretionary Time

name: GK_Per
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GK Per coordinated with XRISM
abstract: GK Per is an accreting white dwarf currently in a dwarf nova outburst. Our reserved ToO observations of GK Per with XRISM were performed 2.5 weeks ago around the outburst maximum (see the orange box in the figure at the first relevant URL). Quick-look data revealed complex Fe I fluorescent line profiles, including unprecedentedly strong Fe I K-beta lines and Compton shoulders accompanied by K-alpha lines - the clearest ever detected in accreting white dwarfs. Accurately modeling these features requires disentangling at least two distinct reflection components. The observations at different stages in this outburst will show simpler iron line profiles and provide key information. Since the iron line flux is fainter by two orders of magnitude in the quiescent state, the observation during quiescence is the best for minimizing exposure time and maximizing the scientific results. We proposed another XRISM ToO, which has been approved and will be performed at the late fading stage of this outburst (see the green line in the figure at the first relevant URL). We aim to model iron emission lines with XRISM data, but at the end of outbursts, the maximum temperature of the plasma exceeds 40--50 keV based on our NuSTAR observation in 2023 (Kimura et al. 2025b) because of the shock heating at the accretion column. Simultaneous hard X-ray observations are indispensable for accurately modeling the continuum and complex iron emission lines. We propose a 40-ks visit of GK Per with NuSTAR to achieve reliable analysis results. We looked for a facility that would conduct observations in hard X-rays, but could not find one. NuSTAR is the only instrument capable of observing hard X-rays at the same time as XRISM DDT.

name: PNV_J19450648p1822422
title: TRACING SHOCK DEVELOPMENT IN A NOVA
abstract: We propose 3x50ks ToO observations of a new bright ($V<7.5$) nova likely to be detected in gamma-rays. The observations will trace the development of shocks within the nova ejecta, constrain the non-thermal particle acceleration and gamma-ray production mechanisms. We will put an upper limit on the particle acceleration efficiency by comparing thermal X-ray and optical to GeV luminosity and search for predicted non-thermal X-rays. Understanding nova shocks is relevant for other shock-powered transients: interacting supernovae, tidal disruption events, stellar mergers. NuSTAR is the only instrument capable of detecting hard X-rays from novae simultaneously with the GeV emission, making it critical to utilize this capability while Fermi continues operations.
subject_category: Proposed ToOs and Directors Discretionary Time

name: 4U_1700p24
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of 4U 1700+24
abstract: 4U 1700+24 is a symbiotic X-ray binary (SyXB) in which a neutron star accretes from the wind of an M2 III giant, HD 154791, at ~0.5 kpc, on the longest known orbital period among SyXBs (~12 yr), viewed nearly pole-on (i~11 deg; Hinkle et al. 2019). The system spends most of its time in a faint, quiescent state (few 1e32 erg/s) punctuated by rare outbursts (dynamic range >200) of unclear origin (wind capture near periastron, transient disc formation, or magnetospheric gating). No coherent pulsations are confirmed, plausibly hidden by the pole-on geometry, and only a handful of outbursts have been caught with broadband instrumentation since the 1970s discovery; the last was detected by Swift in 2014. A previous NuSTAR spectrum showed a candidate cyclotron line (CRSF), but the fit was degenerate: continuum models with and without the line fit equally well (Bozzo et al. 2022), leaving the field unconstrained, though such a high field would matter for the system's accretion history (Ablimit et al. 2023). We report a new outburst detected by SVOM/ECLAIRs (4-150 keV) and EP/WXT (0.5-4 keV), flux already 5x above quiescence: a rare, time-critical chance for the first simultaneous NuSTAR+EP broadband dataset near peak luminosity. NuSTAR's hard-band sensitivity plus EP/FXT soft-band coverage will break the continuum degeneracy limiting the previous CRSF measurement. Science goals: (1) characterize the broadband continuum, search for a high-energy cutoff or Comptonized tail; (2) search for pulsations/QPOs via NuSTAR timing, potentially revealing the NS spin; (3) confirm/refute the candidate CRSF and measure the surface B-field, now with soft-band data to resolve the Bozzo et al. 2022 degeneracy; (4) build a broadband SED testing wind-accretion vs disc formation. Past outbursts lasted only weeks; rapid DDT execution is essential to catch peak flux before the source fades back to quiescence. We checked that no Cycle 12 GO programs have been granted for this target.

name: SAX_J1748d9m2021
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of SAX J1748.9-2021 (4U 1745-203)
abstract: 4U 1745-203 (SAX J1748.9-2021) is an accreting millisecond pulsar located in the Galactic globular cluster NGC 6440 (d=8.5+/-0.4 kpc). Six outbursts have been recorded since 1998 (1998, 2001, 2005, 2010, 2015, and a faint ~13-day outburst in 2017; Pintore et al. 2018), and the source has been quiescent for almost nine years. EP/WXT detected renewed activity, with an unabsorbed flux of (2.4+/-0.5)E-11 erg/cm2/s (0.5-4 keV) on 2026 August 21, rising to (4.7+/-0.8)E-11 erg/cm2/s (0.5-4 keV) on 2026 August 23 (priv. comm. with the EP team), consistent with the onset of a new outburst. Previous bright outbursts reached ~50% of the Eddington luminosity (Pintore et al. 2016), while the faintest one on record (2017) peaked at an order of magnitude lower (~3E36 erg/s, 0.3-70 keV; Pintore et al. 2018). Typical outburst duration is ~30 days. Given the fast rise already observed, a prompt DDT trigger is important to catch the source within the active phase of the outburst. NuSTAR's unique observing capabilities will allow us to investigate both spectral and timing characteristics in hard X-rays. Our goals are the following: (i) to constrain the spectral shape of the source at hard X-rays, measuring the spectral cut-off (if present) of the Comptonization spectrum and thereby the temperature of the electron corona; (ii) to search for the presence of a reflection component in the energy spectrum (see Pintore et al. 2016); (iii) provide an updated timing solution and ephemeris for the optical pulsation search with an approved TNG/SiFAP2 ToO program; (iii) search for type-I bursts and burst oscillations at the known spin frequency since the source is also a prolific type-I burster (25 bursts detected during the single 2015 XMM observation, Pintore et al. 2016, recurrence time ~1 hr).

name: 1E1048d1m5937
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of the magnetar 1E 1048.1-5937
abstract: 1E 1048.1-5937 is a uniquely valuable magnetar for testing whether magnetar activity recurs on a preferred timescale. Since the late 1990s, the source has shown major radiative/torque events separated by roughly five years. Its most recent outburst occurred in July 2022, ~5 yr after the previous event, placing the next expected active epoch in 2027. Our long-term flux and spin-down history highlights this remarkable recurrent behavior (please see light curve in goole drive and Archibald et al. 2020). We request 8x5 ks NuSTAR observations, spaced every three weeks through 31 January 2027, to test whether this apparent ~5 yr cycle persists and to identify the onset of renewed activity. This cadence will establish the current pre-outburst baseline while constraining the onset time of any new event to within ~3 weeks. If activity is detected, we will trigger IXPE to obtain a polarization view of this unusual magnetar; after January, we hope to continue the campaign through a joint IXPE+NuSTAR GO proposal. These short visits are sufficient. At the current 3-79 keV count rate of 0.2 counts s-1 (FPMA+FPMB), 5 ks constrains the 3-10 keV absorption-corrected flux to (4.0 +/- 0.4)x10-12 erg s-1 cm-2 (<10%) and detects the pulse at >10sigma. This DDT request is driven by an unexpected loss of monitoring capability. With Swift/XRT science operations suspended and NICER unavailable, NuSTAR is presently the only practical facility able to provide the repeated sensitive timing and flux measurements required for this experiment. Unfortunately, this situation could not have been anticipated in the regular NuSTAR GO program, because the GO deadline preceded the announcement that Swift would cease science operations. Missing this interval would create a critical gap in a >20-year experiment.

name: SRGAJ174800d5m280826
title: NuSTAR DDT observ ation of SRGA J174800.5-280826
abstract: A new bright X-ray transient was recently discovered in the Galactic Center region by the ART-XC telescope onboard SRG (RA = 267.0020, Dec = -28.1407). The source reached a flux of (3.1e^-11) erg cm^-2 s^-1 in the 4-12 keV band and showed a factor of two increase between consecutive scans separated by about five hours, indicating an active transient event. No bright counterpart is present in archival X-ray catalogues. The source is located close to the unidentified hard X-ray source IGR J17479-2807, although their possible association remains unclear. The hard spectrum, Galactic-plane location, and luminosity (~2e10^35 erg s^-1 assuming 8 kpc) make this transient a promising candidate for a newly discovered accreting compact object. Preliminary information from Einstein Probe observations (private communication) indicates that the source is also very bright in soft X-rays. The FXT data may suffer from pile-up effects, currently under investigation, while a preliminary timing analysis suggests the presence of strong quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). These results are still preliminary and require confirmation with dedicated observations. We propose NuSTAR observations to characterise the broadband spectral and timing properties of this newly discovered transient. The broad energy coverage and high timing capability of NuSTAR will allow us to determine the spectral components, search for hard X-ray tails, study the evolution of the accretion state, and independently confirm the presence of QPOs. These measurements will provide essential constraints on the nature of the compact object and on the accretion geometry, helping to determine whether this source belongs to the population of Galactic neutron-star or black-hole X-ray binaries.

name: XTE_J1739m285
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of SRGA J173953.4-282943 (XTE J1739-285)
abstract: SRGA J173953.4-282943 (XTE J1739-285) is a known transient low-mass X-ray binary hosting an accreting neutron star (NS-LMXB) discovered in 1999 by RXTE (Markwardt et al. 1999). It exhibits recurrent outbursts every 2-7 years, lasting weeks to months, reaching fluxes up to ~5e-9 erg cm-2 s-1. The source is best known for the 1122 Hz burst oscillation candidate reported by Kaaret et al. (2007), which would imply that the system is the fastest-spinning NS known, but more recent work reported the detection of accretion-powered X-ray pulsations at 386 Hz (Beri et al. 2023). The source is also a prolific burster (e.g., Bult et al. 2021). On August 14, 2026 (MJD 61266.30), Einstein Probe (EP/WXT) confirmed a renewed outburst from SRGA J173953.4-282943. Located at R.A. = 264.972 deg, Dec = -28.495 deg (J2000), the source reached an unabsorbed 0.5-4 keV flux of (7.22 +/- 0.69) x 10^-11 erg s^-1 cm^-2. NuSTAR's unique observing capabilities will allow us to investigate both spectral and timing characteristics in hard X-rays. Our goals are the following: (i) Constrain the spectral shape of the source at hard X-rays, measuring the spectral cut-off (if present) of the Comptonization spectrum and thereby the temperature of the electron corona; (ii) Search for the presence of a reflection component in the energy spectrum, i.e., the Iron line at 6.4-6.7 keV and/or the Compton hump at 10-30 keV; (iii) Perform high-precision timing analysis to search for accretion-powered millisecond pulsations, for Type-I X-ray bursts, and for burst oscillations.

name: Crab
title: NuSTAR calibration campaign
abstract: Observations of celestial sources will be undertaken throughout the mission to determine, and then monitor changes to, the calibration of the X-ray observatory. Observations will enable the calibration of absolute flux, spectral sensitivity, point spread function, and the timing capabilities of the observatory as well as the observatory optical alignment. NuSTAR will also participate in cross-calibration campaigns with the Chandra, XMM-Newton, Swift, and Suzaku X-ray observatories.

name: IGR_J17091m3624
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of IGR J17091-3624
abstract: As part of NuSTAR Cycle 12, we have a joint NuSTAR-XRISM monitoring campaign approved (#12228) to monitor the evolution of disk winds in a BH X-ray binary across orders of magnitude changes in accretion rate. One of the proposed targets for our program (IGR J17091-3624) was reported a few weeks ago to have entered an outburst after being detected in optical (ATel 17907) and in X-rays (ATel 17919) by the Einstein Probe. However, before triggering our observing program, we need to obtain a better understanding of the behaviour of this outburst. Given the unavailability of Swift/XRT and NICER, and given that the limited angular resolution of MAXI struggles to resolve this source from nearby bright sources, NuSTAR remains the best observatory for a quick look to assess the evolution of the outburst and the feasibility of triggering our observing program. The source undergoes moderately frequent outbursts. Most recently, the source exhibited a successful outburst in 2022, and a faint (failed) outburst in 2025. We aim to determine whether the current behavior of the source is indicative of a successful outburst (case in which we would also trigger our NuSTAR Cycle 12 program), or of a failed outburst.

name: NGC_1275
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of NGC 1275
abstract: The radio galaxy NGC 1275 (3C 84; z = 0.0176) is undergoing an exceptional MWL outburst that provides a rare opportunity to study particle acceleration and high-energy emission in a nearby misaligned jet. Fermi-LAT first reported high activity on Aug 1 and observed a rapid brightening to a daily flux above 100 MeV of 4.5 10^-6 ph cm-2 s-1 on Aug 4, the highest daily gamma-ray flux ever measured from this source [1,2]. Optical monitoring has found NGC 1275 in one of its brightest states of the past decade, reaching R= 12.71 mag [3]. Most significantly, LHAASO has reported strong TeV emission, detecting the source at ~7.8sigma with an integral flux above 1 TeV of ~0.6 Crab units. Together, these observations establish a rare flaring state from the optical band to TeV energies [4]. NuSTAR is uniquely positioned to measure the hard X-ray spectrum during this event. A contemporaneous 3-79 keV observation will determine whether the GeV-TeV flare is accompanied by spectral hardening or enhanced hard X-ray emission, constrain the location of the IC component, and constrain competing physical scenarios. NuSTAR data will allow us to search for variability down to hour timescale. The detection of X-ray or TeV fast variability would set lower limits on the Doppler factor of the emitting region and challenge radiation/acceleration models given the off-axis nature of the source. The resulting MWL spectral energy distribution will provide critical constraints on the connection between the X-ray and TeV bands. This request is submitted as a DDT because the current event could not reasonably have been anticipated during previous proposal cycles. While NGC 1275 is a known variable AGN, the present outburst combines record-high GeV fluxes, spectral hardening, exceptional optical brightening, and contemporaneous TeV emission detected by LHAASO. This unique combination of observables represents a rare state rather than routine AGN variability and therefore merits rapid ToO follow-up.

name: AT2019wey
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of AT2019wey
abstract: The low-mass black hole X-ray binary AT 2019wey occupies two relatively underexplored territories for IXPE: it has undergone a long outburst in 2019-2025, and it has indications of a fairly low inclination angle (22-30 degrees). Remarkably, during its more than five-year-long outburst, although it occasionally shifted into the soft-intermediate or possibly the high soft state, AT 2019wey predominantly stayed in the hard or hard-intermediate states, making it a rare example of a long-term, hard-only LMXB, comparable to XTE J1752-223. Additionally, detailed spectral analyses (Feng et al. 2022, Draghis et al. 2022) indicate that this source likely has a high spin parameter. After MJD 60750, the source diminished rapidly. Although a dedicated NuSTAR+IXPE campaign was approved at the time, the source could not therefore be followed up as intended. After around MJD 60140, however, the source started rising again. Based on the latest MAXI/GSC lightcurve and has now reached its earlier 2-10 keV flux level of >15 mCrab.Given this rebrightening, an IXPE view of this unique object will, therefore, shed crucial light on stable coronae at low inclinations. However, to maximize the scientific output, we would be required to catch this source in a pure hard state. The latest observation by NuSTAR on March 2026 reveals that the source is in pure hard state, with power law spectral index of 1.7 and marginal reflection component present. Although the MAXI hardness ratio shows a little change in the hardness, now that the source is finally within the IXPE visibility window (Aug 7 - Oct 21, 2026), the lack of simultaneous coverage could make the assessment of spectral state and spectral parameters difficult. Therefore, we propose for a 6 ks NuSTAR observation to asess the spectral state of AT 2019wey. If the source is found to be in the hard state, then we will request a subsequent IXPE observation.

name: 3C033
title: Extragalactic Surveys
abstract: The baseline NuSTAR extragalactic survey is comprised of three components: one deg^2 of the COSMOS field (50ks per position), 0.3 deg^2 of the ECDFS (200ks per position), and a ~3 deg^2 shallow survey (5ks per position), achieved by targeting 100 Swift-BAT identified AGNs.  Models predict that NuSTAR will detect ~200 AGNs in the COSMOS+E-CDF-S surveys and ~19 Compton-thick AGNs. The shallow survey will deliver a sample of serendipitous detection of AGNs in the NuSTAR field of view.

name: EP251020a
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of EP251020a
abstract: We propose a 40 ks observation of the TDE candidate EP251020a to (1) promptly probe its current X-ray state after the solar-conjunction gap, taking advantage of NuSTAR's earliest available visibility window; and (2) use NuSTAR's unique hard-X-ray sensitivity to characterize the high-energy component and constrain its physical origin. EP251020a has undergone dramatic evolution. Since discovery in October 2025 by Einstein Probe Wide-field X-ray Telescope (EP/WXT), the X-ray luminosity increased gradually, followed by a rapid decay of more than two orders of magnitude within 10 days in November, and rebrightened in February 2026. Intriguingly, a double-peaked high-ionization coronal line in optical spectra, [Fe X] 6374, appeared and disappeared together with X-ray emission. This reveals a direct connection between the X-ray activity and the ionizing continuum. To our knowledge, a double-peaked coronal line has never been reported in a TDE, and thus timely multiwavelength follow-up is essential. EP251020a exhibits an unusually hard X-ray spectrum for a TDE candidate. The NuSTAR observation near the November 2025 X-ray peak revealed a hard tail with power law photon index of 3.4+-0.2 up to ~20 keV, which is harder than typical TDEs and may trace a transient Comptonization region, or other high-energy accretion process. The long-term X-ray evolution and spectral properties of EP251020a offer a powerful probe of its emission mechanisms and physical conditions. The scientific objectives of this proposed 40 ks NuSTAR observation are: (1) construct long-term X-ray light curve of EP251020a and test its temporal association with the evolution of high-ionization coronal lines; and (2) measure the 3-20 keV spectrum, constraining the high-energy photon index and searching for spectral evolution relative to the November 2025 bright phase EP251020a is a transient source with unpredictable long-term behaviors, so it could not have been proposed as a GO target.

name: LSXPS_J1709p2651
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of TDE candidate LSXPS J170906.9+265122
abstract: As a part of my Caltech SURF project, under the supervision of Dr. Murray Brightman, with the aim of identifying X-ray transients in SWIFT XRT data, I have discovered LSXPS J170906.9+265122. This source was detected at the end of 2025 and appears to be associated with the optical transient AT2019fdr, which has been suggested to be a tidal disruption event (TDE). These delayed X-rays would be consistent with other optical TDEs. I have been awarded Palomar NGPS time to obtain an optical spectrum of the source this weekend. I request a NuSTAR observation in order to determine in the source is sill x-ray bright and place the optical spectrum in context.

name: NGC6447
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of NGC 6447
abstract: A systematic search of the NEOWISE archive previously revealed a peculiar mid-IR transient in the nucleus of the spiral galaxy NGC 6447 (~100 Mpc), with mid-IR emission steadily rising over 10 years, despite no prior evidence for an AGN. A NuSTAR observation of this source two years ago resulted in the source being only marginally detected. Critically, the inferred X-ray luminosity from that observation is consistent with emission from a population of X-ray binaries (XRBs) in the host galaxy, meaning that the NuSTAR detection alone cannot be taken as a smoking gun for AGN activity. The nature of the nuclear transient in NGC 6447 therefore remains ambiguous. Since that observation, the source has evolved dramatically. Recent SPHEREx observations, analyzed last month after the GO deadline, reveal that the mid-IR flux has more than tripled relative to the epoch of the previous NuSTAR observation. A spectrum obtained last week shows that the flux of optical narrow lines has more than doubled over the same period, suggesting the ongoing formation of the NLR. The fact that the previous NuSTAR observation yielded only a marginal detection, at a luminosity level attributable to XRBs, raises the intriguing possibility that the AGN was genuinely X-ray faint at that epoch - potentially reflecting a physical state in which the X-ray corona is not yet fully established. Such behavior is reminiscent of evidence from Little Red Dots suggesting that AGN in their early phases may be intrinsically X-ray weak. A new 50 ks NuSTAR observation, taken at a epoch when the source is substantially brighter across the IR and optical lines, offers a unique opportunity to test whether the X-ray emission has now risen above the XRB confusion limit, constrain the spectral shape and line-of-sight absorption, and conclusively establish the AGN nature of this transient - shedding light on the X-ray properties and nuclear environment of supermassive black holes in their earliest growth phases.

name: Her_X1
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of Her X-1 coordinated with IXPE
abstract: Her X-1 recently entered an anomalous low state (ALS), a rare and poorly understood phenomenon last observed about 25 years ago. During the ALS, the direct pulsar emission is strongly suppressed, producing an X-ray spectrum fundamentally different from the normal bright state. Recent NuSTAR observations suggest that the spectrum becomes strongly dominated by reflection from the accretion disk. Our approved IXPE DDT observations of this state provide a unique opportunity to isolate the polarization properties of the reflected emission and to verify the NS precession scenario in Her X-1. In the normal state, interpretation of IXPE data is limited by strong degeneracies between direct pulsar emission and the quasi-constant reflected component from the disk, preventing independent constraints on the system geometry and neutron star orientation. During the ALS, however, the pulsar contribution is expected to be strongly reduced, allowing IXPE to directly probe the disk geometry. Simultaneous NuSTAR observations are essential for interpretation of the IXPE data. The key prediction is that the ALS spectrum is reflection dominated and therefore should exhibit polarization properties fundamentally different from those observed in the bright state. NuSTAR is uniquely capable of verifying this reflection-dominated spectrum through its broad energy coverage and sensitivity to the Compton hump and iron-line complex. Without simultaneous broadband spectroscopy, the IXPE polarization signal would remain ambiguous because the relative contributions of direct and reflected emission could not be constrained reliably in 2-8 keV band. Current monitoring shows that the ALS Main-on flux (~5x10-11 erg/s/cm2) is comparable to a normal Short-on state and sufficient for high-quality NuSTAR spectroscopy. We therefore request a simultaneous NuSTAR observation coordinated with the approved IXPE DDT campaign.

name: SN2026obc
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of SN2026obc
abstract: We request a NuSTAR DDT observation of the recently discovered Type Icn supernova SN 2026obc. Type Icn supernovae are an exceptionally rare class of interaction-powered transients that provide a unique window into extreme mass loss from massive stars immediately prior to core collapse. They are characterized by rapidly evolving light curves and narrow carbon and oxygen emission lines, generally interpreted as signatures of interaction between the supernova ejecta and hydrogen- and helium-poor circumstellar material (CSM). The physical origin of Type Icn supernovae remains poorly understood due to the small number of known events and the lack of multiwavelength observations. X-ray observations provide one of the most direct probes of the interaction region, constraining the CSM density, shock power, ejecta properties, and CSM composition. These quantities are often highly degenerate when inferred from optical data alone. Despite their importance, no Type Icn supernova has yet been detected in X-rays. Recent theoretical Type Icn models (e.g., Inoue et al. 2025) predict that, during the earliest phases of interaction, the emergent X-ray spectrum should be dominated by hard X-rays (>10 keV) because the dense CSM is still optically thick to soft X rays. As a result, observations above 10 keV are expected to provide the most sensitive probe of the interaction-powered emission. NuSTAR is uniquely capable of testing these predictions and searching for the first hard X-ray detection of a Type Icn supernova.

name: EP260507b
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of EP260507b
abstract: e request NuSTAR DDT observation of EP260507b, a jetted tidal disruption event (TDE) candidate now in radio outburst detected by MeerKAT. This event offers a unique, time-critical opportunity to constrain jet-accretion physics in a transient regime inaccessible to AGN studies. EP260507b had a 0.5-4.0 keV (WXT) observed flux of ~1e-10 erg/s/cm^2 at its peak (ATel #17789), and after a power-law like decline, it now reaches a plateau at ~5e-12 erg/s/cm^2 (0.3-10.0 keV in FXT). Its 0.3-10.0 keV (FXT) spectra can be fitted by a power-law with index of 1.4-1.7 (private communication). The power-law index is similar as those in all X-ray counterparts of the rare "jetted TDE" family: Swift J164449.3+573451, Swift J2058.4+0516, Swift J1112.2-8238. A faint optical counterpart has been found, which helps confirm its coordinates. The detections in soft X-ray, radio and optical bands suggest that EP260507b can be a newly-born jetted event and most likely to be created by a tidal disruption event, and regardless of its mechanism, this case represents a rarely-seen birth of a jet in distant universe. While Einstein Probe constrains the thermal accretion disk (0.5-4 keV), NuSTAR's 3-79 keV coverage uniquely probes the hot corona and jet-driven inverse Compton emission, breaking degeneracies in Comptonization models. Early hard X-ray data are historically sparse for TDEs, this ToO fills a crucial temporal gap before source fade. If a NuSTAR DDT observation is approved, another MeerKAT radio observation will be performed simultaneously, which will put constraints on the accretion-jet coupling and accretion state transitions: radio synchrotron and hard X-ray Comptonization trace fundamentally different zones, allowing us to measure the accretion rate feeding the jet and constrain the Lorentz factor via their correlation. This synergy is essential and time-dependent (the radio/X-ray window may close within weeks).

name: ATLAS26gre
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of ATLAS26gre (AT2026ofr), possible SN Ia in NGC 5102
abstract: ATLAS26gre (AT2026ofr) is a newly discovered faint transient in NGC 5102 in 4 Mpc. This source was discovered on 2026-06-05.13 (see URL below) by ATLAS. There was no detection a week prior at 2026-05-31.88. However, the source type is currently unknown. Given that NGC 5102 is a lenticular S0 galaxy. So if this is a supernova, we expect that it could be a thermonuclear source, which would make it the closest Type Ia supernova since SN 2014J (distance of ~3.6 Mpc).

name: Cyg_X1
title: NuSTAR observation of Cyg X-1 coordinated with XRISM
abstract: Cygnus X-1 is the prototypical wind-fed black-hole high-mass X-ray binary and a benchmark source for accretion, disk reflection, and focused stellar winds. XRISM will observe Cyg X-1 from 2026-06-04T02:21:00 to 2026-06-10T21:17:00, covering approximately one full 5.6-day binary orbit. This XRISM program is designed as a legacy high-resolution dataset: Resolve will provide phase-resolved Fe-K spectroscopy of neutral fluorescence and highly ionized Fe XXV/XXVI absorption, enabling tomography of the focused wind and tests of whether seconds-scale Fe-K variability is driven by wind photoionization/recombination or by inner accretion-flow variability. However, XRISM alone cannot determine the hard X-ray continuum above 10 keV, where the Comptonized emission, reflection hump, and high-energy spectral curvature are measured most directly. Simultaneous NuSTAR coverage is therefore essential. Without NuSTAR, the XRISM Fe-K absorption and fluorescence diagnostics must be interpreted against a continuum and reflection model that is only weakly constrained at high energies, limiting our ability to separate changes in the ionized wind from changes in the intrinsic continuum, coronal properties, and disk reflection. NuSTAR provides the only focusing hard-X-ray capability above 10 keV during this XRISM window. A simultaneous NuSTAR observation will constrain the 10--79 keV continuum, reflection hump, and high-energy cutoff, providing the broadband context needed to infer coronal parameters and reflection-related black-hole spin constraints. The joint XRISM+NuSTAR dataset will therefore transform this observation from a high-resolution Fe-K study into a complete broadband legacy dataset for wind-fed black-hole accretion.

name: Her_X1
title: NuSTAR monitoring observations of Her X-1
abstract: HerX-1 is a known binary system with over 55 years history of X-ray observations. Typically, the source is bright enough to be detected even by all-sky monitors. However, few times during its history, it has entered to so called Anomaly Low State (ALS). The last time it was heppened ~25 years ago. Now the source is on its way to another ALS. ART-XC and NuSTAR have been tracking the flux change for the past 3 months, observing the source at the flux maximum of the precessional phase (a series of bservations every 35 days). name: XTE_J1859p083
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of the X-ray pulsar XTE J1859+083
abstract: XTE J1859+083 is a poorly explored accretion-powered X-ray pulsar that exhibits a combination of observational properties not commonly seen in accreting neutron stars (Salganik et al. 2021, MNRAS 509, 5955-5963), currently in outburst (Atel #17730,17770). Despite its relatively featureless energy spectrum, the source shows complex pulse profiles. Remarkably, these profiles display only mild evolution across the NuSTAR energy band, compared to other known X-ray pulsars. Such behaviour appears to be shared only by one other source, EXO 2030+375, whose magnetic field strength is likewise poorly constrained (Thalhammer et al. 2024, A&A, 688, A213), suggesting a potentially distinct class of systems with atypical emission geometry or magnetic configuration. The pulsed fraction is nearly constant across the energy range, in contrast to most Galactic X-ray pulsars with detected cyclotron lines where a significant increase of the pulsed fraction toward higher energies is typically observed. This unusual behaviour may provide a key diagnostic to distinguish between high- and low-magnetic-field scenarios suggested for the source (Salganik et al. 2021). An additional peculiarity is that the optical companion appears significantly reddened placing it in a highly absorbed region. Moreover, the distance remains poorly constrained (~3-12 kpc, likely >7 kpc), which introduces substantial uncertainty in luminosity estimates and accretion regime classification. The main questions are whether the pulse profile changes with luminosity, which would constrain the viewing geometry (inclination and magnetic obliquity; see, e.g., Maniadakis et al. 2025, A&A, 700, A70), and whether the spectrum remains featureless, develops cyclotron lines, which in some systems become more prominent at lower luminosities (Kong et al 2021, ApJL, 917, L38), or appear as signature in the pulsed fraction spectra (Ambrosi et al. 2026, A&A, 709, A42)

name: Cyg_X3
title: DDT observations of Cyg X-3
abstract: Cyg X-3 is a microquasar known for its bright, recurrent flares observed from radio to gamma-rays. Recently, LHAASO detected transient PeV gamma-ray emission at the highest photon energy ever detected from Galactic sources, suggesting Cyg X-3 may be one of the most energetic Galactic PeVatrons. Such flares are likely tied to relativistic plasmoids and particles in the jet. In early February 2025, Cyg X-3 entered an ultra-soft/radio-quenched state, following a hard phase that began in August 2024. Historically, these states precede major flares with peak radio fluxes up to ~20 Jy. The duration of the ultra-soft/radio state varied from several days to several months in the past. In addition to the continuous monitoring by RATAN-600 (radio), soft X-ray (MAXI), hard X-ray (Swift/BAT), GeV (Fermi-LAT) and TeV (LHAASO) bands, our collaboration is planning a major observation campaign to capture the transition phase to a major flare by VLBA, SMA, XRISM and Astri-Mini (TeV) telescopes. We request NuSTAR DDT observations for this rare opportunity to observe the quench-to-flare transition phase in coordination with other telescopes. NuSTAR's broadband X-ray data will be uniquely valuable for multi-wavelength SED modeling (from radio to TeV gamma-rays) and complement high-resolution Fe line spectroscopy (with XRISM DDT to be requested) by characterizing the continuum X-ray emission.

name: EP260324a
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of EP260324a - an emerging hard component
abstract: We propose a 40 ks urgent ToO observation of the transient EP260324a with NuSTAR. The goal is to utilize NuSTAR's unique hard X-ray capabilities to characterize the source's spectrum above 2 keV, in order to clarify the physical origin of the high-energy emission from this new TDE candidate. Following our successful two XMM-Newton triggers, continued critical monitoring with EP's Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) has revealed a new, pivotal phase in the source's evolution. Since mid-April, the soft X-ray 0.5-2keV flux has begun a gradual decline, accompanied by ongoing spectral hardening. However, a direct comparison between our two XMM-Newton observations indicates a highly significant and counterintuitive trend: while the soft X-ray flux decreases, the hard X-ray emission above 2 keV has become markedly stronger. This apparent anti-correlation between the soft and hard X-ray bands strongly suggests a fundamental shift in the accretion flow or the emergence of a new radiative component. We keep monitoring this TDE with EP-FXT, and a simultaneous observation with NuSTAR to extend the broadband coverage into the hard X-ray regime is crucial for constraining the high-energy emission mechanism. A coordinated EP-FXT/NuSTAR campaign is essential to capitalize on this unique opportunity. The scientific objectives of this proposed 40 ks NuSTAR observation are: (1)Construct a broadband SED: Combining NuSTAR's hard X-ray data with soft X-ray data will enable complete spectral energy distribution modeling from 0.5 keV to several tens keV. (2)Measure the 2-30 keV spectrum, to determine the high-energy photon index and detect any spectral cutoff or curvature, which will directly distinguish between emission mechanisms.

name: 4U_1909p07
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of the Supergiant X-ray binary 4U 1909+07 coordinated with XRISM
abstract: We request one 20 ks NuSTAR DDT observation of the persistent Supergiant X-ray binary 4U 1909+07 to enhance our already approved XRISM Cycle 2 program. The XRISM observation (ObsID 202043010) will be performed during the week of May 3, where the aim is to search for a Compton shoulder of the Fe Kalpha line previously claimed with Chandra. NuSTAR will extend our constraint of the spectral continuum up to 70 keV, further constraining the spectral continuum that has known curvature outside the XRISM bandpass. This will allow an accurate measurement of the spectral continuum to further probe the Fe fluorescent region with XRISM.

name: V4641_SGR_BACKGROUND
title: A BROADBAND X-RAY SURVEY OF THE ULTRA-HIGH-ENERGY GAMMA-RAY EMISSION AROUND SUPER-PEVATRON MICROQUASAR V4641 SGR
abstract: Microquasars are an emerging class of Galactic PeVatrons powered by relativistic jets from stellar-mass black holes. Among the five known TeV microquasars, V4641 Sgr is the only super-PeVatron detected up to ~1 PeV, indicating particle acceleration to ~10 PeV. We propose a broadband X-ray survey of the TeV lobes discovered by HAWC and spatially resolved by H.E.S.S. This survey aims to establish the nature of the diffuse X-ray emission reported by XRISM, identify hard X-ray knots as the most energetic particle acceleration sites, and detect thermal X-rays at jet termination sites. We will map the X-ray flux, nH and spectral index (vs. TeV and CO images) and determine the gamma-ray emission and particle acceleration mechanisms of this super-PeVatron through SED analysis of hard X-ray knots.
subject_category: Non-ToO Supernovae, SNRs, and Galactic diffuse emission

name: AT2026fgk
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of AT2026fgk - afterglow of GRB 260310A
abstract: Long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are brief powerful explosions that launch ultra-relativistic jets and are believed to arise from the core-collapse of massive stars. The low-luminosity LGRBs have a low prompt-emission efficiency but can have their afterglow kinetic energies Ek exceed the prompt luminosity by ~2 orders of magnitude. These can arise from a dirty fireball scenario or from a standard ultra-relativistic jet viewed off-axis. Distinguishing these mechanisms has remained difficult as nearby GRBs are rare - with an observed rate of ~1/year nearby GRBs with an even lower rate for the low-lumunosity LGRBs (just two examples in the past ~20 years - GRB 190829A & GRB 171205A). The physical origin of low prompt efficiency has never been clearly resolved. Both of these models predict X-ray emission but the key discriminant is the morphology of the X-ray light curve and the timing of the jet-break. NuSTAR's 3-79 keV bandpass uniquely probes the hard X-ray afterglow at 10-30 days post-burst, and allows it to distinguish when the break occurs along with a detailed SED modelling. At these late times, the synchrotron cooling break is expected to migrate through or below the NuSTAR band. Sampling the SED across the wavelengths, and tracking its evolution is needed to carefully estimate the micro and macro parameters - like E_k, distribution of shock internal energies, electron power-law index, circumburst density - of the outflow from the GRB. The study of these parameters, in the case of low-luminosity GRBs, is best possible for nearby events (redshift z <0.5).

name: GS_1354m64
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of GS 1354-64
abstract: The current outburst of GS~1354-64 is exhibiting several unusual features. Over the past week, the source showed rapid flux variability, with the X-ray brightness doubling from ~200 mCrab to ~400 mCrab and then declining back to ~200 mCrab within only 3-4 days. Much of this rapid evolution was not covered by NuSTAR observations. The most recent NuSTAR observation (January 30) suggests that the source may have transitioned out of the hard state; however, this interpretation remains uncertain because more recent HXMT observations report QPOs consistent with the hard or hard-intermediate states. This behavior is atypical and may indicate that the source has either not yet reached the soft state or remained there only briefly. To track the rapid and unpredictable spectral evolution of the source, we request six(6) NuSTAR DDT monitoring observations of GS~1354-64, each with exposures of ~5-10 ks, spaced at intervals of one to two weeks. To avoid conflicts with any ongoing NuSTAR GO program targeting the source, these DDT observations can be deferred by up to one week whenever a scheduled GO observation is present. We are flexible with the proposed monitoring and are fully willing for the observations to be executed only as NuSTAR scheduling allows. Our simulations show that exposures of 5-10 ks are sufficient to constrain the broadband spectral properties at expected NuSTAR count rates of ~100-150 counts s-1 (the source is currently steady at ~200 counts s-1). At these exposure lengths, no additional ground-station contacts are required. This monitoring program will also serve as a useful test case for NuSTAR's capability to perform short, high-cadence monitoring observations of rapidly evolving transients in the future.

name: 1ES_1927p654
title: TRACKING THE UNUSUALLY COOL CORONA DURING A REAL-TIME JET LAUNCH IN AN AGN
abstract: 1ES~1927+654 is an enigmatic changing look active galaxy (CL-AGN) which has recently shown a nascent bi-polar radio jet on pc scales, evolving at a speed of 0.2c, a unique event of jet formation and evolution in real-time from an AGN. Contemporaneous to the jet formation, multiple snapshots of NuSTAR observations have detected a cool corona kT = 8 keV. These extraordinary discoveries reveal intimate connections between jet formation and the heating/cooling rates in the corona (connected by magnetic fields). Here we propose to monitor this interesting source bimonthly with NuSTAR for the next 1 year with 40 ks exposure per snapshot (=240ks total) to track the long-term changes in the coronal temperature and slope as the jet forms and evolves.

name: 3C_390d3
title: HARD X-RAY LEVERAGE FOR XRISM: NUSTAR ON 3C 390.3
abstract: We request a 50-ks NuSTAR observation of the bright broad-line radio galaxy 3C390.3, scheduled contemporaneously with a 170-ks XRISM/Resolve pointing in late April 2026. NuSTAR will anchor the hard-X-ray continuum and high-energy cutoff (Ecut) in the XRISM epoch and quantify the weak-reflection state. With Ecut constrained, we will fit finite-column reprocessing models to the Compton hump to test whether the dominant reflector is Compton-thin or near/Compton-thick, turning "weak reflection" into a physical constraint on the cold reprocessor and coronal illumination geometry.

name: Kepler
title: NuSTAR calibration campaign
abstract: Observations of celestial sources will be undertaken throughout the mission to determine, and then monitor changes to, the calibration of the X-ray observatory. Observations will enable the calibration of absolute flux, spectral sensitivity, point spread function, and the timing capabilities of the observatory as well as the observatory optical alignment. NuSTAR will also participate in cross-calibration campaigns with the Chandra, XMM-Newton, Swift, and Suzaku X-ray observatories.

name: GC_BRIDGE_CLOUD
title: CAPTURING PEAK X-RAY LUMINOSITY OF GALACTIC CENTER MOLECULAR CLOUD THE BRIDGE: STORYTELLER OF A PAST SGR A* OUTBURST
abstract: After 25 years of X-ray brightening, Bridge has become the brightest giant molecular cloud in the Galactic center, due to X-ray reflection of a past Sgr A* outburst ~200 years ago. The Bridge is the only molecular cloud that will allow us to investigate the full profile of a Sgr A* illumination event. Its peak luminosity and duration are essential information to characterize the past Sgr A* outburst that illuminated this molecular cloud. A 100 ks simultaneous NuSTAR and XMM-Newton observation will most efficiently measure the peak X-ray luminosity of the Bridge. Characterizing past Sgr A* outbursts is a necessary step towards understanding the physical mechanisms that triggered major outbursts from a quiescent supermassive black hole, e.g. a tidal disruption event.
subject_category: Non-ToO Supernovae, SNRs, and Galactic diffuse emission

name: Her_X1
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of Her X-1 in anomalous low state
abstract: Swift/BAT and MAXI have revealed that the soft X-ray flux of Her X-1 has been decreasing to quite low levels (Mihara et al., ATEL 17607), it is about to enter an "Anomalous Low" States. Only five such events were observed until today. Anomalous low states (ALs) are thought to be associated with absorption along our line of sight to the neutron star caused by a change of the inclination of the disk. Anomalous lows are connected with extremely interesting physical phenomena in this accreting binary system, such as precession of the accretion disk, precession of the neutron star itself, and the so far not well understood interactions between both entities. We ask for TOO observations of Her X-1 during the next three ongoing 35d precessional cycles of the accretion disk: For each of those three cycles we ask for three pointings during the time of the (extrapolated) Main-Ons of 10 ks, in three consecutive orbits. The next Turn-On was expected to occur on 8 February 2026, the first pointing could be done on 11 February 2026, further two pointings 1.7 days and 3.4 days later. If we detect pulsations, we can measure the pulse period, which will have significantly changed (a dramatic spin-down is expected). Possibly pulse profiles can be produced which may allow to infer the times of turn-ons, since there is a tight relationship between the pulse profile and the 35d phase. Doing this for a few 35d cycles in a row, we could get a measure of the cycle lengths, which is expected to be significantly shorter then normally. We also can attempt to generate an energy spectrum from which we can determine the effektive absorption. We stress that NuSTAR is the perfect instrument for these observations due to its high energy response. The proposing team includes J. Wilms, L. Ducci, N. Shakura, K. Postnov, R. Rothschild and other members of the XMAG collaboration.

name: GS_1843p00
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GS 1843+00
abstract: GS 1843+00 is a Be/X-ray binary hosting a 29.5 s accreting neutron star pulsar (Israel et al. 2001). The system was discovered in 1988 and exhibited multiple X-ray outbursts until 2010. After ~16 years of quiescence, MAXI detected renewed X-ray activity from the direction of GS 1843+00 in February 2026 (MJD 61098; ATel #17706). A follow-up observation with NuSTAR on 2026 March 10-11 confirmed the ongoing outburst and showed that the pulsar was accreting at a flux level of 5.8e-9 erg/s/cm2 (ATel #17722). This corresponds to a luminosity of 7e37 erg/s (assuming a distance of 10 kpc), placing the source above the typical critical luminosity where significant changes in the accretion column structure and pulse morphology are expected. At this luminosity, the pulse profile appears complex and differs significantly from the simpler shapes reported during the 1997 and 2009 outbursts observed with RXTE (see figure in URL below). In particular, the measured pulse fraction is relatively low (~10% in the 3-79 keV band), even lower than the pulse fraction observed during the 1997 outburst at a flux of 3.9e-9 erg/s/cm2. Such behaviour is uncommon among accreting X-ray pulsars at comparable luminosities and may indicate changes in the emission geometry during the present outburst. Given the rarity of the outburst and the limited broadband observations available so far, we request an additional NuSTAR observation during the current activity episode to investigate the evolution of the pulse morphology and spectral properties of the pulsar. name: SDSS_J093922d89p3
title: A TESTBED TO MODEL X-RAY EMISSION OF PUZZLING JWST AGN: STUDY OF NEARBY ANALOG SUPER-EDDINGTON AGN WITH NUSTAR
abstract: We propose NuSTAR observations of two hyper-Eddington AGN (for a total of 350 ks), together with XMM-Newton simultaneous observations (for a total of 80 ks). The targets have very extreme values of Eddington ratio (> 200). So far, just one source with a similarly high value of Eddington ratio is known and has been observed with NuSTAR. This proposal offers a unique opportunity to deeply characterize the broad-band X-ray spectra of extremely peculiar AGN which, according to most theoretical models, are analogues to those recently observed by JWST. The observation of the proposed targets will provide a rare opportunity to explore the innermost regions of highly accreting AGN and test various models proposed for super-Eddington accretion.

name: Crab
title: NuSTAR calibration campaign
abstract: Observations of celestial sources will be undertaken throughout the mission to determine, and then monitor changes to, the calibration of the X-ray observatory. Observations will enable the calibration of absolute flux, spectral sensitivity, point spread function, and the timing capabilities of the observatory as well as the observatory optical alignment. NuSTAR will also participate in cross-calibration campaigns with the Chandra, XMM-Newton, Swift, and Suzaku X-ray observatories.

name: EP260324a
title: PROBING COSMOLOGICAL BLACK HOLES WITH NUSTAR AND NICER AS THEY IGNITE RELATIVISTIC JETS
abstract: Following NICER+NuSTAR's recent success in capturing the spectro-timing variability of the farthest stellar tidal disruption event (TDE) to-date we propose ToO monitoring observations of a future relativistic TDE, i.e., a system with a newborn relativistic jet pointed directly along our line of sight. Our main goals are 1) to establish the relativistic nature of the future transient by measuring its luminosity and variability, and 2) combine NICER+NuSTAR data with our approved multi-frequency radio data to perform multi-epoch spectral energy distribution modelings to shed light on the underlying jet physics. Our scientific goals require high-cadence monitoring for weeks and hard X-ray coverage making NICER + NuSTAR ideal facilities for the proposed study.

name: AT2026fgk
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of AT2026fgk - afterglow of GRB 260310A
abstract: Long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are brief powerful explosions that launch ultra-relativistic jets and are believed to arise from the core-collapse of massive stars. name: UGC_4211
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of UGC 4211 coordinated with XMM
abstract: We request a NuSTAR DDT observation of UGC 4211 to coordinate with an approved 36 ks XMM observation scheduled for 2026 April 5 (PI: Koss). UGC 4211 hosts the closest confirmed dual AGN (230 pc, 0.32"), discovered through multi-wavelength spectroscopy including HST/STIS, VLT/MUSE AO, Keck/OSIRIS, and ALMA (Koss+23, ApJL 942, L24). Both nuclei show unresolved ALMA 230 GHz continuum at 10 pc scales, but the system exhibits a 0.7-1.3 dex deficit in intrinsic X-ray emission relative to the tight mm/X-ray correlation established for 98 BAT AGN (Ricci+23). This is the most extreme outlier in the sample, suggesting either severely underestimated obscuration, spectral blending from two unresolved sources, or significant variability. The last NuSTAR observation was in 2017, nearly 9 years ago. Since then, ALMA (45, 100 GHz), VLA (15, 22 GHz), and VLBA (5, 15, 22 GHz) observations have been approved for April 2026 (or happened in April), along with JWST/NIRSPEC. This coordinated multi-wavelength campaign could not have been proposed through the standard GO program because the multi-facility scheduling only became finalized recently. NuSTAR is essential for anchoring the hard X-ray continuum above 10 keV, constraining the reflection component and Compton-thick obscuration that XMM alone cannot measure. The previous Chandra+NuSTAR analysis assumed a single source and found log(NH)=22.95, but if the true column density is log(NH)~23.8 (as predicted by the mm/X-ray correlation), the reflection-dominated spectrum above 10 keV is critical to distinguish this from a lower-NH model. Joint XMM+NuSTAR broadband fitting (0.3-79 keV) will provide the first accurate decomposition of the blended X-ray emission and test for variability relative to the 2017 baseline, while quasi-simultaneous radio and mm data anchor the cross-wavelength comparisons.

name: IRAS_18293m0941
title: PROBING THE NATURE OF THE MICROBLAZAR CANDIDATE IRAS 18293-0941
abstract: IRAS 18293-0941 (XGPS-3) was identified as a high-mass X-ray binary candidate but remains poorly studied. Archival VLA data reveal a non-thermal radio spectrum with a one-sided jet, resembling a blazar. ZTF photometry confirms a ~5.73-day periodicity, supporting a binary nature, while VLT spectra suggest a high-mass companion with strong emission lines. XMM-Newton and NICER detect a persistent X-ray source consistent with a high-mass X-ray binary. The lack of hard X-ray data prevents confirmation of a non-thermal component. We propose a 180 ks NuSTAR observation to search for non-thermal emission above 10 keV, which would confirm relativistic jets and support the microblazar nature of this source.

name: SWIFTJ1648d6m2313
title: Extragalactic Surveys
abstract: The baseline NuSTAR extragalactic survey is comprised of three components: one deg^2 of the COSMOS field (50ks per position), 0.3 deg^2 of the ECDFS (200ks per position), and a ~3 deg^2 shallow survey (5ks per position), achieved by targeting 100 Swift-BAT identified AGNs.  Models predict that NuSTAR will detect ~200 AGNs in the COSMOS+E-CDF-S surveys and ~19 Compton-thick AGNs. The shallow survey will deliver a sample of serendipitous detection of AGNs in the NuSTAR field of view.

name: ESO138m1
title: PROBING THE STRUCTURE OF AGN TORI WITH NUSTAR
abstract: Variability in line-of-sight column density (NH,los) is critical for understanding the structure of the obscuring material in AGN. While studies suggest a clumpy torus, variability constraints for obscured AGN remain sparse, with most limited to months-to-years timescales and obscured (NH=10^22-24 cm^-2) but non-Compton-thick (NH>10^24 cm^-2) sources. This pilot study proposes a NuSTAR large program (750 ks) to perform the first systematic search for short-term variability in five nearby (z<0.02) Compton-thick Seyfert 2 galaxies, which exhibit year-scale NH,los variability. By probing days-to-weeks timescales, we will determine whether obscuration changes arise from compact clouds near the SMBH or larger-scale structures, providing critical constraints on the geometry of the AGN tori.

name: LSXPS_J150746d7m5927
title: UNVEILING THE NATURE OF NEWLY DETECTED MEV GALACTIC SOURCES
abstract: We propose to observe 3 new candidates MeV emitting Galactic sources with NuSTAR for a total of 210ks. These sources have been detected for the very first time in the 20-200 MeV range and reside in the Galactic plane (b<5 deg). However, the lack of good-quality X-ray data hampers the source classification (e.g. SNR, PSR, PWN), and the characterization of their spectral properties (spectral index, shape, and flux). The excellent sensitivity of NuSTAR will enable us to fully characterize the SED from 3 keV - 200 MeV. Composing a broadband SED of these objects will enable us to (i) determine the nature of these newly discovered sources: (ii) perform a detailed study of their SED and compute their energetics.

name: 1A_0535m66
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of A0538-66 near periastron
abstract: The Be/X-ray binary (BeXRB) A0538-66 is one of the most unusual accreting neutron star systems known. After decades of quiescence, it has recently re-entered an active phase, with bright X-ray outbursts detected in September 2025 and February 2026 in MAXI monitoring. These events occur near periastron (P_orb ~ 16.65 days) and reach fluxes of ~0.15-0.2 Crab in the 4-10 keV band. The February 2026 event is brighter and exhibits a secondary flare, indicating that the system can sustain multiple accretion episodes within a single orbital passage. Unlike typical Be/X-ray binaries with multi-day outbursts, A0538-66 shows very short flares (<1 day), so daily-averaged monitoring (e.g., MAXI) can underestimate peak luminosity and miss the brightest phase without rapid-response observations. The neutron star likely has a low magnetic field (B ~ 10^10-10^11 G), far below typical BeXRB pulsars (>10^12 G), but this remains observationally unconstrained as no cyclotron line has been detected. This suggests A0538-66 may represent a distinct accretion regime bridging classical BeXRBs and weak-field systems. It has never been observed in the 10-79 keV band during an outburst. A NuSTAR observation would provide the first hard X-ray spectrum in its active state, enabling a search for cyclotron features and detection of hard X-ray pulsations, if present. Recent optical spectroscopy from SALT (October 2025, private communication) shows unusual absorption features, indicating major changes in the circumstellar disk, likely linked to renewed X-ray activity. We will coordinate NuSTAR with SALT for near-simultaneous spectroscopy, enabling us to probe disk evolution and its connection to accretion. Combining NuSTAR hard X-ray data with optical spectroscopy will provide a rare direct view of disk-accretion coupling in BeXRBs. The observation could not be proposed through the GO program because the source became active after decades of quiescence and was not predictable.

name: GS_1843p00
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GS 1843+00
abstract: GS 1843+00 is a Be/X-ray binary hosting a 29.5 s accreting neutron star pulsar (Israel et al. 2001). The system was discovered in 1988 and exhibited multiple X-ray outbursts until 2010. After ~16 years of quiescence, MAXI detected renewed X-ray activity from the direction of GS 1843+00 in February 2026 (MJD 61098; ATel #17706). A follow-up observation with NuSTAR on 2026 March 10-11 confirmed the ongoing outburst and showed that the pulsar was accreting at a flux level of 5.8e-9 erg/s/cm2 (ATel #17722). This corresponds to a luminosity of 7e37 erg/s (assuming a distance of 10 kpc), placing the source above the typical critical luminosity where significant changes in the accretion column structure and pulse morphology are expected. At this luminosity, the pulse profile appears complex and differs significantly from the simpler shapes reported during the 1997 and 2009 outbursts observed with RXTE (see figure in URL below). In particular, the measured pulse fraction is relatively low (~10% in the 3-79 keV band), even lower than the pulse fraction observed during the 1997 outburst at a flux of 3.9e-9 erg/s/cm2. Such behaviour is uncommon among accreting X-ray pulsars at comparable luminosities and may indicate changes in the emission geometry during the present outburst. Given the rarity of the outburst and the limited broadband observations available so far, we request an additional NuSTAR observation during the current activity episode to investigate the evolution of the pulse morphology and spectral properties of the pulsar. The proposed observation will allow us to (i) measure luminosity-dependent changes in the hard X-ray continuum shape and cutoff energy, (ii) study the evolution of the pulse profile morphology and pulse fraction, (iii) perform detailed timing analysis to track spin-period evolution, and (iv) carry out pulse-phase-resolved spectroscopy to probe the emission geometry at different luminosity levels.

name: XTE_J1739m285
title: NEXTEPP -- A NUSTAR EXPANSION OF TRANSIENTS FROM EINSTEIN PROBE PULSATORS
abstract: We propose a NuSTAR+NICER follow-up program of newly discovered Einstein Probe sources of interest. We focus our program on weakly and highly magnetized accreting neutron star pulsators in order to exploit the design of the proposed facilities at full and maximize their scientific return. Our program will guarantee the minimum scheduling stress for the proposed facilities, facilitating the observational efforts and maximizing its scientific outcome. The scientific return will characterize spectral and timing behaviour of accreting X-ray pulsars aiming towards population studies that would solve the tension between models and observations from this class sources.
