name: 1A_1118m61
title: Continuued NuSTAR DDT monitoring of Be XRP 1A 1118-61
abstract: Swift/BAT detected an X-ray brightening from the Be XRP 1A 1118-61 (2025 January 17, MJD 61057; ATel 17608). A NuSTAR observation (2026 January 2) measured Lx=4e+37 erg/s (3-79 keV), confirming the onset of a giant (Type II) outburst (ATel 17626). Starting from January 26, the source began to decline. A second NuSTAR observation (2026 February 21) caught the source already in the decaying phase at 3e+36 erg/s (3-79 keV). Recent SRG/ART-XC monitoring (2026 March) shows that the source continues to decay in the 4-12 keV band and has already faded by about a factor of 3 since the last NuSTAR observation. Based on the decay profiles observed in previous outbursts, we expect the source to reach the 10^35 erg s^-1 level within the next ~2 weeks. It is particularly important because low-luminosity observations of A 0535+262 (Tsygankov et al. 2019), an XRP with similar ~50 keV CRSF, showed that the continuum changed dramatically while the CRSF energy remained constant. In that source, a double-humped spectrum emerged at ~1e+35 erg/s. Since 1A 1118-61 shows a CRSF at ~55 keV, it is an excellent target to test whether the same occurs here. It is expected in this regime that, once the luminosity drops, the accretion flow overheats the atmosphere (Mushtukov et al. 2021). Strong spectral changes are already seen between the two NuSTAR observations of 1A 1118-61: as the Lx dropped from 4x10^37 to ~3x10^36 erg/s, the plasma became hotter and more optically thin (kTe: 7 -> 10 keV, au: 7 -> 3) and the continuum flattened. A third observation is needed to complete tracking of this spectral transformation into the very low-luminosity regime. The proposed observation will constrain physical conditions leading to the formation of the two-humped spectral shape, characterize the ~50 keV CRSF and its luminosity variability. We therefore propose a single 60 ks NuSTAR observation. This exposure is sufficient to obtain high signal-to-noise broadband spectra.

name: GRS_1758m258
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GRS 1758-258 coordinated with XRISM
abstract: We will observe the Galactic black hole X-ray binary (BHXB) GRS 1758-258 with XRISM from 2026 Mar. 22 for about 1 day (net exposure ~40 ks), based on our approved AO-2 proposal. We request a simultaneous 20 ks observation with NuSTAR. When we began preparing the XRISM AO-2 proposal, the deadline for the NuSTAR Cycle 11 call for proposals had already passed, and coordinated NuSTAR time was not available within the AO-2 framework (unlike in AO-3). Therefore, we are requesting this as a DDT request. The XRISM observation aims to search for disk winds and investigate relativistic effects near the black hole through high-resolution spectroscopy with Resolve. A previous Suzaku study reported a possible ultra-fast wind with a velocity of ~0.1c (Reynolds et al. 2018), more than an order of magnitude faster than typical winds in BHXBs. If confirmed, it would be the highest-velocity wind detected in a BHXB, providing strong evidence that ultrafast outflows can be launched from stellar-mass black holes. Such a velocity cannot be explained by thermal driving, implying a magnetically driven wind. Resolve will enable us to search for and characterize wind absorption lines and measure key parameters such as the velocity, column density, and ionization parameter. To constrain the wind launching radius, however, we must accurately determine the ionizing X-ray luminosity (>9 keV for Fe K-shell electrons). Since XRISM covers energies only up to ~12 keV, NuSTAR is essential to constrain the hard X-ray spectral profile. In addition, reflection features, including a broad Fe Kalpha line and a Compton hump around 20-30 keV, were reported previously (e.g., Jana et al. 2022). Modeling these features with relativistic reflection models can constrain the disk truncation radius and black hole spin. NuSTAR observations of the reflection hump, combined with the narrow spectral features resolved by XRISM, will enable a comprehensive study of the accretion flow and outflow structure in this system.

name: Her_X1
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of Her X-1 in anomalous low state
abstract: Swift/BAT and MAXI have revealed that the soft X-ray flux of Her X-1 has been decreasing to quite low levels (Mihara et al., ATEL 17607), it is about to enter an "Anomalous Low" States. Only five such events were observed until today. Anomalous low states (ALs) are thought to be associated with absorption along our line of sight to the neutron star caused by a change of the inclination of the disk. Anomalous lows are connected with extremely interesting physical phenomena in this accreting binary system, such as precession of the accretion disk, precession of the neutron star itself, and the so far not well understood interactions between both entities. We ask for TOO observations of Her X-1 during the next three ongoing 35d precessional cycles of the accretion disk: For each of those three cycles we ask for three pointings during the time of the (extrapolated) Main-Ons of 10 ks, in three consecutive orbits. The next Turn-On was expected to occur on 8 February 2026, the first pointing could be done on 11 February 2026, further two pointings 1.7 days and 3.4 days later. If we detect pulsations, we can measure the pulse period, which will have significantly changed (a dramatic spin-down is expected). Possibly pulse profiles can be produced which may allow to infer the times of turn-ons, since there is a tight relationship between the pulse profile and the 35d phase. Doing this for a few 35d cycles in a row, we could get a measure of the cycle lengths, which is expected to be significantly shorter then normally. We also can attempt to generate an energy spectrum from which we can determine the effektive absorption. We stress that NuSTAR is the perfect instrument for these observations due to its high energy response. The proposing team includes J. Wilms, L. Ducci, N. Shakura, K. Postnov, R. Rothschild and other members of the XMAG collaboration.

name: AT2019wey
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of AT2019wey coordinated with XRISM
abstract: One of the most important, unresolved systematic uncertainties in the field of relativistic reflection studies of accreting stellar-mass black holes (BH) is the effect of unresolved, unaccounted-for narrow spectral features on the ability to measure system parameters, including BH spin and viewing inclination. The sensitivity and energy resolution of Resolve guarantee an immediate and definitive resolution to this issue. Owing to its low inclination, the ideal source for this study is the galactic BH low-mass X-ray binary AT2019wey. We obtained a 30ks XRISM observation of this source as a Cycle 2 proposal with the goals of identifying narrow absorption features in the Fe band, breaking parameter degeneracies, and quantifying the impact of narrow features on BH spin and inclination measurements. However, given the reduction in flux of the source in recent months, it is unclear whether XRISM alone can reliably constrain the underlying continuum. Hence, we request a NuSTAR DDT observation of the source, simultaneous with the XRISM observation, to offer improved constraints on the ionizing flux (energies above ~9keV) and on the coronal properties of the source. We note that XRISM Cycle 2 did not offer the option for joint NuSTAR proposals. Also, given the flux of the source at the time, the continuum could have been constrained by XRISM alone. While this source has been observed by NuSTAR in the past, given its short-term variability, using archival observations is not feasible for the purpose of this study.

We ask for TOO observations of Her X-1 during the next three ongoing 35d precessional cycles of the accretion disk: For each of those three cycles we ask for three pointings during the time of the (extrapolated) Main-Ons of 10 ks, in three consecutive orbits. The next Turn-On was expected to occur on 8 February 2026, the first pointing could be done on 11 February 2026, further two pointings 1.7 days and 3.4 days later. If we detect pulsations, we can measure the pulse period, which will have significantly changed (a dramatic spin-down is expected). Possibly pulse profiles can be produced which may allow to infer the times of turn-ons, since there is a tight relationship between the pulse profile and the 35d phase. Doing this for a few 35d cycles in a row, we could get a measure of the cycle lengths, which is expected to be significantly shorter then normally. We also can attempt to generate an energy spectrum from which we can determine the effektive absorption. We stress that NuSTAR is the perfect instrument for these observations due to its high energy response. The proposing team includes J. Wilms, L. Ducci, N. Shakura, K. Postnov, R. Rothschild and other members of the XMAG collaboration.

name: LV_MUS
title: ARE THERE BEXRBS LURKING AMONG LUMINOUS LONE BE STARS?
abstract: Be stars, with circumstellar decretion disks have been increasingly posited to have hidden companions. In X-rays, they are mostly studied as BeXRBs which have thus far shown predominantly transient behaviour with their extremely luminous outbursts. However, recent research has shown that persistent X-ray emission at low luminosities outside of outburst is the default. The low luminosity end of the distribution of High Mass X-ray Binaries is thus populated by low luminosity BeXRBs. The luminosity distribution of Be stars on the other hand shows a handful of luminous systems which overlap in luminosity with the least luminous BeXRBs. We propose for follow-up of hitherto known to be isolated Be stars which populate this overlap region in luminosity, with 60ks of NuSTAR observations each.

name: GS_1354m64
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of GS 1354-64
abstract: The current outburst of GS~1354-64 is exhibiting several unusual features. Over the past week, the source showed rapid flux variability, with the X-ray brightness doubling from ~200 mCrab to ~400 mCrab and then declining back to ~200 mCrab within only 3-4 days. Much of this rapid evolution was not covered by NuSTAR observations. The most recent NuSTAR observation (January 30) suggests that the source may have transitioned out of the hard state; however, this interpretation remains uncertain because more recent HXMT observations report QPOs consistent with the hard or hard-intermediate states. This behavior is atypical and may indicate that the source has either not yet reached the soft state or remained there only briefly. To track the rapid and unpredictable spectral evolution of the source, we request six(6) NuSTAR DDT monitoring observations of GS~1354-64, each with exposures of ~5-10 ks, spaced at intervals of one to two weeks. To avoid conflicts with any ongoing NuSTAR GO program targeting the source, these DDT observations can be deferred by up to one week whenever a scheduled GO observation is present. We are flexible with the proposed monitoring and are fully willing for the observations to be executed only as NuSTAR scheduling allows. Our simulations show that exposures of 5-10 ks are sufficient to constrain the broadband spectral properties at expected NuSTAR count rates of ~100-150 counts s-1 (the source is currently steady at ~200 counts s-1). At these exposure lengths, no additional ground-station contacts are required. This monitoring program will also serve as a useful test case for NuSTAR's capability to perform short, high-cadence monitoring observations of rapidly evolving transients in the future.

name: Mrk609
title: Extragalactic Surveys
abstract: The baseline NuSTAR extragalactic survey is comprised of three components: one deg^2 of the COSMOS field (50ks per position), 0.3 deg^2 of the ECDFS (200ks per position), and a ~3 deg^2 shallow survey (5ks per position), achieved by targeting 100 Swift-BAT identified AGNs.  Models predict that NuSTAR will detect ~200 AGNs in the COSMOS+E-CDF-S surveys and ~19 Compton-thick AGNs. The shallow survey will deliver a sample of serendipitous detection of AGNs in the NuSTAR field of view.

name: 1LHAASO_J0206p4302U
title: NUSTAR OBSERVATIONS OF DARK LHAASO SOURCES
abstract: This project expects to perform NuSTAR X-ray Observations on three targets in 1LHAASO J0212 Complex. Firstly, the observations are expected to map this region and discover any putative source related to the TeV emission: next, this study also plans to search for periodical pulsar signals in the observation: meanwhile, we propose to perform detailed and comprehensive spectral analyses with help of NuSTAR and other telescopes. All these could provide information to study the origin of such mysterious TeV emission at high Galactic latitude, and possibly bring new understandings about high energy astrophysics in the Milky Way.
subject_category: Non-ToO Supernovae, SNRs, and Galactic diffuse emission

name: 3C172
title: WHAT FRACTION OF POWERFUL RADIO GALAXIES AT 0.5 < Z < 1 ARE COMPTON-THICK ?
abstract: A Chandra survey of high-redshift, powerful radio 3CRR AGN found narrow-line radio galaxies to have 10-1000 times lower X-ray luminosity than quasars with comparable extended radio luminosity. If orientation-dependent obscuration, as in Unification models, causes radio galaxies' X-ray weakness, then 50% of 3CRR AGN are obscured and ~20% are Compton thick (CT). This is a higher fraction than typically surmised and implies significant under-estimation of the high-luminosity AGN population. However, the X-ray spectra of candidate CT 3CRR sources are soft suggesting, instead, low obscuration and luminosity and implying an X-ray weak AGN population inconsistent with Unification. We propose NuSTAR observations of five 3CRR CT candidates to distinguish between CT and X-ray-weak possibilities.

name: WISEA_J0247p0752
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of WISEA J024728.03+075250.2 - possible association with GRB 260226A
abstract: Gamma-ray bursts are brief, powerful explosions that launch ultra-relativistic outflows. Despite decades of extensive research, the detailed physics governing these sources remains partially understood. A major unresolved issue concerns the physics of jet production: How are these relativistic outflows launched, and what role do magnetic fields play in shaping them? Addressing these questions requires connecting jet properties inferred from afterglow light curves with measurements of prompt-emission polarisation. NuSTAR's 3-79 keV bandpass uniquely probes the hard X-ray afterglow at 10-15 days post-burst, when emission is dominated by the forward shock in the normal-to-post-jet-break decay phase. At these late times, the synchrotron cooling break is expected to migrate through or below the NuSTAR band, enabling direct measurement of the cooling frequency and electron index parameters degenerate in soft X-rays alone. Late-time hard X-ray detections enable testing for inverse-Compton contributions that standard synchrotron models cannot explain. In the absence of Swift, localization of GRBs has become more challenging. The unique capabilities of NuSTAR will allow us to solve this problem. Earlier this week NuSTAR performed two short observations tiling the Fermi LAT position associated with GRB 260226A. A possible detection at log F(2-10)/cgs ~ -12.8 +/- 0.2 coincides with WISEA J024728.03+075250.2. The requested deeper observation will allow us to verify the origin of the detection. If a similar flux level could be recovered then the detection most likely originates from an AGN. If the observation results in a non detection, this would be in line with the fading X-ray flux during afterglow, and would further support the hypothesis of a GRB origin. In the latter case, this will be the first GRB to be localized with NuSTAR.

name: OAO_1657m415
title: INVESTIGATING THE PUTATIVE ACCRETION WAKE IN OAO 1657 415 DURING LATE ORBITAL PHASES
abstract: We propose a total (XMM: 80 ks+NuSTAR: 80 ks) observation of OAO 1657 415 at two orbital phases (i) during the onset of a putative accretion wake (&#981: = 0.45 0.55: 40 ks) and (ii) when the accretion wake is heavily obscuring the line of sight (&#981: = 0.75 0.85: 40 ks). We will characterize the wake through detailed spectral modelling, exploring whether they are composed of unstable dense gas filaments or a temporary (but more stable) accretion disk is formed when the accretion flow collides with a shock in the accretion wake region. In the unlikely case of the wakes not being detected, this would still provide valuable insight, as it would contradict hydrodynamical predictions, necessitating further investigation into alternative accretion mechanisms.

name: PSR_J2229p6114
title: TARGET-OF-OPPORTUNITY NUSTAR OBSERVATIONS OF HIGH-B RADIO PULSARS: SEARCHING FOR MAGNETAR METAMORPHOSES
abstract: We propose for a 150~ks (50 ks x 3) NuSTAR observational program to investigate magnetar-like behavior in high-magnetic field rotation-powered pulsars following timing glitches. Using near-daily radio monitoring observations with CHIME/Pulsar, we will trigger NuSTAR observations within ~48 hours of a glitch: the broadband coverage of NuSTAR will probe the presence of a power law tail (hard X-rays), a key signature of magnetars. The proposed observational cadence will track the evolution of the power law tail throughout the outburst and test the consistency with magnetospheric cooling scenarios in magnetars. The detection of the hard X-ray component will solidify the connection between high magnetic field rotation-powered pulsars and magnetars, unifying the neutron star zoo.
subject_category: Proposed ToOs and Directors Discretionary Time

name: GS_1843p00
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GS 1843+00
abstract: GS 1843+00 (Ginga 1843+009) is a Be/X-ray binary hosting a 29.5 s accreting X-ray pulsar (Israel et al. 2001). The system was discovered by Ginga in 1988 and exhibited multiple X-ray outbursts until 2010. No significant activity has been reported over the past 16 years. On 2026 February 27 (MJD 61098), MAXI detected renewed X-ray activity from the direction of GS 1843+00 (ATel #17706), with the 2-20 keV flux reaching ~28 mCrab. The source is currently accreting at ~50 mCrab level (MAXI 2-20 keV) on MJD 61102. This provides a unique opportunity to study GS 1843+00 with NuSTAR. Accreting X-ray pulsars are key laboratories for studying accretion column physics under extreme magnetic fields. Their broadband spectra typically exhibit a power-law continuum with a high-energy cutoff and, in some cases, cyclotron resonant scattering features (CRSFs), which provide a direct measurement of the neutron star magnetic field strength. However, GS 1843+00 remains poorly characterized in the hard X-ray band. A tentative indication of a CRSF near ~20 keV has been suggested in previous studies, but it has not been firmly established yet. NuSTAR's 3-79 keV bandpass and high sensitivity in the hard X-ray regime enable a comprehensive broadband characterization of the pulsar. The proposed observation will allow us to (i) accurately measure the hard X-ray continuum and constrain the cutoff energy, (ii) conduct a sensitive search for CRSFs over a broad energy range, (iii) perform detailed timing analysis of the 29.5 s pulsations, and (iv) carry out pulse-phase-resolved spectroscopy to probe the emission geometry and magnetic-field configuration. Detection of a CRSF would directly constrain the neutron star magnetic field strength, while a robust upper limit would still provide important constraints on the accretion physics of this system. Given the long recurrence time (~16 years), this is a rare opportunity to study the pulsar with NuSTAR.

name: 1E_1547d0m5408
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of the magnetar 1E 1547.0-5408 coordinated with IXPE
abstract: The phenomenon of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) is one of the most tantalizing mysteries in astronomy. However, the mechanism of how magnetars initiate FRBs is poorly understood. In October 2022, this magnetar exhibited FRBs and short X-ray bursts again. During this magnetar outburst, ToO observations and time series analyses with NICER and NuSTAR revealed a pair of glitches that occurred before and after FRBs, associated with a burst forest, providing valuable insights into this mystery. Hence, this proposal aims to prompt and high-cadence X-ray monitoring during an outburst of transient magnetars to investigate their X-ray behaviours and to search for glitches similar to those of SGR 1935+2154 and also for FRB-associated X-ray bursts.

name: EP260126a
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of EP260126a
abstract: EP260126a was discovered by the EP/WXT on 2026 January 26 as a fast X-ray transient. Early EP/FXT follow-up at 0.8 and 1.7 days post-trigger revealed a fading X-ray light curve with a decay slope of approximately -1.3. No gamma-ray or optical counterpart has been identified. Subsequent VLA and EP/FXT observations uncovered a contemporaneous radio and X-ray rebrightening about 25 days after the trigger. While rebrightenings a few days after the burst have been observed in some GRBs and are often interpreted as refreshed shocks or late-time energy injection, a delayed X-ray bump on a month timescale is highly unusual. Such delayed rebrightening could instead indicate a different physical origin, potentially including interaction with a structured circumburst medium, or even a relativistic tidal disruption event (TDE). The source will continue to be monitored with EP/FXT to track its soft X-ray (0.5-10 keV) evolution. Combined FXT and NuSTAR observations will thus provide a simultaneous broadband X-ray spectrum, enabling us to distinguish between these scenarios, which requires broadband spectral diagnostics extending to hard X-rays. The presence (or absence) of a hard X-ray component will directly test whether the emission is consistent with synchrotron afterglow radiation, inverse Compton processes, or a harder, possibly coronal or accretion-powered spectrum as expected in TDE-like scenarios. A measurement of the broadband spectral slope and any high-energy cutoff will provide decisive constraints on the emission mechanism and energy dissipation process.

name: Crab_deepbkgd
title: NuSTAR calibration campaign
abstract: Observations of celestial sources will be undertaken throughout the mission to determine, and then monitor changes to, the calibration of the X-ray observatory. Observations will enable the calibration of absolute flux, spectral sensitivity, point spread function, and the timing capabilities of the observatory as well as the observatory optical alignment. NuSTAR will also participate in cross-calibration campaigns with the Chandra, XMM-Newton, Swift, and Suzaku X-ray observatories.

name: LSXPS_J104152d1m5746
title: UNVEILING THE NATURE OF NEWLY DETECTED MEV GALACTIC SOURCES
abstract: We propose to observe 3 new candidates MeV emitting Galactic sources with NuSTAR for a total of 210ks. These sources have been detected for the very first time in the 20-200 MeV range and reside in the Galactic plane (b<5 deg). However, the lack of good-quality X-ray data hampers the source classification (e.g. SNR, PSR, PWN), and the characterization of their spectral properties (spectral index, shape, and flux). The excellent sensitivity of NuSTAR will enable us to fully characterize the SED from 3 keV - 200 MeV. Composing a broadband SED of these objects will enable us to (i) determine the nature of these newly discovered sources: (ii) perform a detailed study of their SED and compute their energetics.

name: IGR_J00370p6122
title: UNVEILING THE PROPERTIES OF THE SUPERGIANT X-RAY BINARY IGR J00370+6122 WITH NUSTAR
abstract: IGR J00370+6122 is an enigmatic and poorly studied supergiant X-ray binary. It has one of the most eccentric orbits of its class and it shows a strong orbital modulation. IGR J00370+6122 is unconventional and of particular interest for evolutionary studies and for understanding the accretion mechanism that causes its X-ray behaviour. Nonetheless, it has been scarcely observed above 10 keV. Therefore, we propose the first NuSTAR observation of IGR J00370+6122 to perform the most sensitive spectral and timing study to measure fundamental parameters such as the spin period and magnetic field strength, with the ultimate goal of understanding its nature.

name: ESO138m1
title: PROBING THE STRUCTURE OF AGN TORI WITH NUSTAR
abstract: Variability in line-of-sight column density (NH,los) is critical for understanding the structure of the obscuring material in AGN. While studies suggest a clumpy torus, variability constraints for obscured AGN remain sparse, with most limited to months-to-years timescales and obscured (NH=10^22-24 cm^-2) but non-Compton-thick (NH>10^24 cm^-2) sources. This pilot study proposes a NuSTAR large program (750 ks) to perform the first systematic search for short-term variability in five nearby (z<0.02) Compton-thick Seyfert 2 galaxies, which exhibit year-scale NH,los variability. By probing days-to-weeks timescales, we will determine whether obscuration changes arise from compact clouds near the SMBH or larger-scale structures, providing critical constraints on the geometry of the AGN tori.

name: 1A_1118m61
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of the transient Be/X-ray binary 1A 1118-61
abstract: 1A 1118-61 is a transient Be/X-ray binary hosting a neutron-star pulsar (spin ~405-409 s) in a ~24 d orbit around the Be star He 3-640/Wray 793, at a distance of ~5 kpc. The source is currently undergoing a bright giant outburst. A Swift/XRT observation (ATel #17627) on 2026 Jan 23 detected the source clearly in 1-10 keV. The spectrum is well described by an absorbed thermal Comptonization model with best-fit NH ~ 0.8 x 10^22 cm^-2 and an observed 1-10 keV flux ~ 4 x 10^-9 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Timing analysis shows coherent pulsations at ~409 s with a double-peaked pulse profile. The hard X-ray emission is extreme: Swift/BAT (15-50 keV) on 2026 Jan 28 is ~0.25 ct cm^-2 s^-1 (>1 Crab), and the BAT light curve indicates the source is near the outburst peak. NuSTAR is uniquely suited to exploit this rare opportunity because it provides sensitive broadband coverage up to 79 keV, required to measure the cyclotron resonance scattering feature (CRSF; previously reported near ~55 keV) and to track its pulse-phase and luminosity dependence. NuSTAR observed the source on 2026 Jan 24 (ATel #17626) and detected a ~53.8 keV cyclotron line, but the flux and spectrum are evolving rapidly. A second NuSTAR observation is needed to (i) perform high-S/N phase-resolved spectroscopy of the CRSF and continuum geometry, (ii) test for luminosity-dependent shifts in the line parameters, (iii) measure energy-dependent pulse profiles and absorption dips, and (iv) search for transient timing features such as QPOs. This observation could not have been proposed through the regular GO program because giant outbursts in Be/X-ray binaries are unpredictable. Using the BAT rate and a hard spectrum (Gamma ~ 1), WebPIMMS predicts ~5.8 x 10^2 c s^-1 (FPMA+FPMB, 3-79 keV; before deadtime). A 40 ks exposure will yield >1 x 10^7 counts, enabling 16-bin phase-resolved spectroscopy with high S/N. We request ~40 ks within ~2 weeks to secure a high-quality NuSTAR dataset during the current outburst.

name: ABELL_1750N
title: ABELL 1750 - EXAMINING A TRIPLY MERGING CLUSTER ALONG A COSMIC FILAMENT WITH NUSTAR, SOFT X-RAY, AND LENSING MASS MAPS
abstract: We will use NuSTAR to examine the complex Abell 1750 galaxy cluster, potentially one of the brightest clusters in hard X-rays (from previous RXTE constraints), and probe ongoing non-thermal processes. This will be the first NuSTAR observation of a triple cluster. Clusters are powerful probes of astrophysics and cosmology, but the pressure/energy budget of individual systems can scatter them from the predictions of mass-observable relations. Hard X-rays shed light onto such deviations by constraining the cosmic ray density and pressure. Using a weak-lensing mass map, soft X-ray, and NuSTAR data, we will model the non-thermal contribution to A1750's pressure budget, and using VLASS 1.4GHz maps will produce an upper limit magnetic field strength.

name: IGR_J14175m4641
title: DISSECTING THE TORUS: A GOLDEN SAMPLE OF HEAVILY OBSCURED AGN WITH MULTI-EPOCH NUSTAR AND XMM OBSERVATIONS
abstract: Studies of heavily obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) suggest that the torus that causes the obscuration is clumpy, rather than uniform. The line-of-sight column density (NHlos) of the obscuring material should vary over weeks to months, but such an evidence has been observed only in a few X-ray detected AGN, due to lack of large samples of heavily obscured AGN with multi-epoch observations, which are key to characterize the obscuring material surrounding accreting SMBHs. We propose for a joint NuSTAR-XMM monitoring of 3 nearby Compton thick AGN with small torus covering factor and NH_los significantly larger than the torus average NH. Through this monitoring, we expect to measure significant variability in NHlos, and obtain the most accurate picture of nuclear obscuration in low-z AGN.

name: ESO138m1
title: PROBING THE STRUCTURE OF AGN TORI WITH NUSTAR
abstract: Variability in line-of-sight column density (NH,los) is critical for understanding the structure of the obscuring material in AGN. While studies suggest a clumpy torus, variability constraints for obscured AGN remain sparse, with most limited to months-to-years timescales and obscured (NH=10^22-24 cm^-2) but non-Compton-thick (NH>10^24 cm^-2) sources. This pilot study proposes a NuSTAR large program (750 ks) to perform the first systematic search for short-term variability in five nearby (z<0.02) Compton-thick Seyfert 2 galaxies, which exhibit year-scale NH,los variability. By probing days-to-weeks timescales, we will determine whether obscuration changes arise from compact clouds near the SMBH or larger-scale structures, providing critical constraints on the geometry of the AGN tori.

name: 1ES_1927p654
title: TRACKING THE UNUSUALLY COOL CORONA DURING A REAL-TIME JET LAUNCH IN AN AGN
abstract: 1ES~1927+654 is an enigmatic changing look active galaxy (CL-AGN) which has recently shown a nascent bi-polar radio jet on pc scales, evolving at a speed of 0.2c, a unique event of jet formation and evolution in real-time from an AGN. Contemporaneous to the jet formation, multiple snapshots of NuSTAR observations have detected a cool corona kT = 8 keV. These extraordinary discoveries reveal intimate connections between jet formation and the heating/cooling rates in the corona (connected by magnetic fields). Here we propose to monitor this interesting source bimonthly with NuSTAR for the next 1 year with 40 ks exposure per snapshot (=240ks total) to track the long-term changes in the coronal temperature and slope as the jet forms and evolves.

name: GS_1826m238
title: DDT observations of the clocked burster GS 1826-238 coordinated with VLA
abstract: GS 1826-24, aka 'the clocked burster', is a persistently accreting, bursting neutron star that is famous for its highly regular type-I X-ray bursting behavior. For over 30 years it remained in a hard state during which it demonstrated the closest agreement with thermonuclear burning models among the over 125 known burst sources. However, in 2014, it suddenly transitioned to a soft and the regularity of its bursts ceased (Chenevez+2016, ApJ 818). After 10 years in a soft state, GS 1826-24 has now yet again returned to a hard state (ATel #17251) and its highly repetitive bursts are back (ATel #17245). We propose 2x20 ks NuSTAR DDT observations to accompany an approved Chandra DDT (PI Kajava) and a submitted VLA DDT (PI Russel) to leverage the highly unique regular bursting behavior of the source to: 1) measure the speed of its jet from the delay between X-ray burst peaks and associated radio jet flare peaks (Russel+2024, Nature 627) - and to do this for individual bursts while probing if/how the obtained speeds correlate with the mass-accretion rate between bursts; 2) understand the jet launch mechanism by observing the response of the radio jet to a burst simultaneously with burst-induced changes in the X-ray emitting disk and corona (Speicher+2020, MNRAS 499; Speichler+2024, ApJ 976) to bursts; 3) measure the burst recurrence time simultaneously with the accretion emission between bursts, and compare these to values measured before 2014, to test theoretical predictions that the accretion geometry determines how a neutron star is heated and cooled (Inogamov & Sunayaev, 2010).

name: Her_X1
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of Her X-1 in anomalous low state
abstract: Swift/BAT and MAXI have revealed that the soft X-ray flux of Her X-1 has been decreasing to quite low levels (Mihara et al., ATEL 17607), it is about to enter an "Anomalous Low" States. Only five such events were observed until today. Anomalous low states (ALs) are thought to be associated with absorption along our line of sight to the neutron star caused by a change of the inclination of the disk. Anomalous lows are connected with extremely interesting physical phenomena in this accreting binary system, such as precession of the accretion disk, precession of the neutron star itself, and the so far not well understood interactions between both entities. We ask for TOO observations of Her X-1 during the next three ongoing 35d precessional cycles of the accretion disk: For each of those three cycles we ask for three pointings during the time of the (extrapolated) Main-Ons of 10 ks, in three consecutive orbits. The next Turn-On was expected to occur on 8 February 2026, the first pointing could be done on 11 February 2026, further two pointings 1.7 days and 3.4 days later. If we detect pulsations, we can measure the pulse period, which will have significantly changed (a dramatic spin-down is expected). Possibly pulse profiles can be produced which may allow to infer the times of turn-ons, since there is a tight relationship between the pulse profile and the 35d phase. Doing this for a few 35d cycles in a row, we could get a measure of the cycle lengths, which is expected to be significantly shorter then normally. We also can attempt to generate an energy spectrum from which we can determine the effektive absorption. We stress that NuSTAR is the perfect instrument for these observations due to its high energy response. The proposing team includes J. Wilms, L. Ducci, N. Shakura, K. Postnov, R. Rothschild and other members of the XMAG collaboration.

name: ABELL_1750C
title: ABELL 1750 - EXAMINING A TRIPLY MERGING CLUSTER ALONG A COSMIC FILAMENT WITH NUSTAR, SOFT X-RAY, AND LENSING MASS MAPS
abstract: We will use NuSTAR to examine the complex Abell 1750 galaxy cluster, potentially one of the brightest clusters in hard X-rays (from previous RXTE constraints), and probe ongoing non-thermal processes. This will be the first NuSTAR observation of a triple cluster. Clusters are powerful probes of astrophysics and cosmology, but the pressure/energy budget of individual systems can scatter them from the predictions of mass-observable relations. Hard X-rays shed light onto such deviations by constraining the cosmic ray density and pressure. Using a weak-lensing mass map, soft X-ray, and NuSTAR data, we will model the non-thermal contribution to A1750's pressure budget, and using VLASS 1.4GHz maps will produce an upper limit magnetic field strength.
subject_category: Galaxy clusters and extragalactic diffuse objects

name: 4FGL_J2015d4p6556
title: UNCOVERING THE MOST POWERFUL JETS THROUGH COSMIC TIME
abstract: From the 4LAC catalog, we have chosen four high-latitude blazars at z>2.5, that currently lack NuSTAR observations. These blazars, classified as FSRQs, are very likely prototypical MeV blazars: powerful blazars hosting massive black holes releasing most of their energy in the MeV band. MeV blazars play a crucial role in constraining the space density of massive black holes in the early Universe. NuSTAR observations will enable us to detect the proposed sources in the hard X-ray band, accurately measure the spectral shape and flux, and probe the onset of inverse Compton emission. These properties are crucial for determining the jet power and the electron population driving the emission. Therefore, we request 132 ks of NuSTAR time to observe all four sources.

name: IGR_J14175m4641
title: DISSECTING THE TORUS: A GOLDEN SAMPLE OF HEAVILY OBSCURED AGN WITH MULTI-EPOCH NUSTAR AND XMM OBSERVATIONS
abstract: Studies of heavily obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) suggest that the torus that causes the obscuration is clumpy, rather than uniform. The line-of-sight column density (NHlos) of the obscuring material should vary over weeks to months, but such an evidence has been observed only in a few X-ray detected AGN, due to lack of large samples of heavily obscured AGN with multi-epoch observations, which are key to characterize the obscuring material surrounding accreting SMBHs. We propose for a joint NuSTAR-XMM monitoring of 3 nearby Compton thick AGN with small torus covering factor and NH_los significantly larger than the torus average NH. Through this monitoring, we expect to measure significant variability in NHlos, and obtain the most accurate picture of nuclear obscuration in low-z AGN.

name: IGR_J16318m4848
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of IGR J16318-4848 coordinated with XRISM
abstract: IGR J16318-4848 is a Compton-thick (logNH > 24.2) high-mass X-ray binary, widely regarded as the most obscured X-ray source in our Galaxy. In Feb. 2026, we will target IGR J16318 with XRISM for a net exposure of 100 ks, to study X-ray absorption and reflection in the Compton-thick regime, and unveil the nature of the obscuring medium, whose origin remains debated; with proposed scenarios including a dense stellar wind, a B[e]-star decretion disk, and leftover supernova ejecta. With XRISM, we expect to see a pure-reflection spectrum with prominent fluorescent lines and one of the best-resolved Fe Ka Compton shoulders. Yet, critical complementary information is encoded in the hard X-ray spectrum above the XRISM range, as revealed in previous NuSTAR campaigns: The same obscuring medium can be probed through the prominent Compton reflection hump (10-30 keV), whereas above 30 keV, NuSTAR can characterise the intrinsic source emission, which is fully unaccessible in the XRISM band. IGR J16318 is known to be highly variable on ks-timescales (Barragn+09; Jain+09), but this variability has been commonly related to accretion disk instabilities (Walter+03), claimed to induce no changes to the cold-reflection spectrum (Ballhausen+20). However, in preparation of our XRISM observation, we discovered unreported spectral variability (Fe Ka/Compton hump ratio) between low- and high-flux states in archival NuSTAR data, motivating the need for simultaneous XRISM+NuSTAR coverage to exploit the full power of a combined spectral analysis. The Fe Ka Compton shoulder (XRISM) and the Compton reflection hump (NuSTAR) together provide a uniquely powerful probe to discriminate between competing 3D radiative-transfer models of Compton-thick reflection, while NuSTAR can also probe the deeply buried intrinsic source emission. We kindly request 30 ks of net NuSTAR DDT time, scheduled simultaneously with our XRISM observation, to secure coverage of at least one low-flux and one high-flux state.

name: UGC_9618N
title: PROBING THE LINK BETWEEN MASER EMISSION AND OBSCURATION WITH NUSTAR
abstract: Water megamaser emission is produced in hot and dense enviroments near AGN. While few of these sources are known, they have a significant overlap with another very elusive source population: Compton-thick AGN. Recent observational and theoretical advances have suggested a potential origin for this connection: that maser emission is produced in a warped disk, placed at the inner edge of the torus, which is responsible for both high obscuration and intense reflection features. Here, we propose to observe 4 megamasers with joint NuSTAR and XMM observations, in order to start increasing the small (and biased) sample of megamasers covered by NuSTAR. Through this work, we will test the current theory, potentially opening the door to placing constraints on torus size based on maser observations.

name: 1E_1547d0m5408
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of the magnetar 1E 1547.0-5408 coordinated with IXPE
abstract: The phenomenon of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) is one of the most tantalizing mysteries in astronomy. However, the mechanism of how magnetars initiate FRBs is poorly understood. In October 2022, this magnetar exhibited FRBs and short X-ray bursts again. During this magnetar outburst, ToO observations and time series analyses with NICER and NuSTAR revealed a pair of glitches that occurred before and after FRBs, associated with a burst forest, providing valuable insights into this mystery. Hence, this proposal aims to prompt and high-cadence X-ray monitoring during an outburst of transient magnetars to investigate their X-ray behaviours and to search for glitches similar to those of SGR 1935+2154 and also for FRB-associated X-ray bursts.

name: NGC6240
title: UNVEILING THE DUAL AGN IN NGC 6240: A JOINT XRISM AND NUSTAR INVESTIGATION OF MERGER DRIVEN OBSCURATION
abstract: NGC 6240 is a nearby (100~Mpc) major galaxy merger with a closely separated pair of heavily obscured AGN that provides a Rosetta Stone to study rapid, merger-triggered growth hidden behind a thick veil of obscuring gas. We propose a ToO observation to coincide with a possible upcoming 225 ks XRISM observation of the same galaxy to study the connection between luminosity and obscuration via variability. This is a once-in-a-mission opportunity to learn how massive black holes grow in the final stages of a galaxy merger. Prior NuSTAR observations reveal that NGC 6240 varies in luminosity by 20% on 20 ks timescales, suggesting that its absorbing column varies over years. NuSTAR+XRISM will enable the first kinematic study of Fe Ka combined with the high energy sensitivity of NuSTAR.

name: GS_1354m64
title: NuSTAR DDT monitoring of the black hole X-ray binary GS 1354-64 during outburst
abstract: Study of Temporal and Spectral Properties of the Black Hole X-ray Binary GS 1354-64 During Outburst Scientific Justification: GS 1354-64 (BW Cir) is a transient X-ray binary hosting a stellar-mass black hole. An X-ray outburst was reported by MAXI on 25 December 2025 and Swift/XRT on 7 January 2026. We request 60 ks of NuSTAR observations, divided into three 20 ks pointings separated by 10-day intervals, to cover the peak and decay phases. Most BHXBs are transients spending long periods in quiescence. Outbursts, likely triggered by accretion disk instabilities, allow unique tests of accretion physics under extreme conditions. X-ray luminosity can rise from L   1030-31 erg s-1 to L  1038-39 erg s-1, with strong spectral and rapid timing variability. Typically, BHXBs follow a "q"-shaped hardness-intensity evolution, transitioning from low-hard through intermediate to high-soft states and back. Some outbursts, however, remain in the hard state ("failed outbursts"), and the reason for this behavior is unclear (e.g., GS 1354-64, SWIFT J1753.5-0127). GS 1354-64, a dynamically confirmed BHXB with a G0-5 III donor in a ~2.5-day orbit, has exhibited outbursts in 1987, 1997, and 2015. In these events, it remained in a luminous hard X-ray state (peak luminosity of LX > 0.15 Ledd) without transitioning to the soft state. Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) with increasing centroid frequency indicate strong inner-disk variability. These unusually luminous hard-state outbursts challenge standard accretion models. NuSTAR's 3-79 keV sensitivity is ideal to track spectral evolution, detect possible state transitions, and study timing features such as QPOs and dips. Observing this outburst will help to study whether the source exhibits possible X-ray state changes during the outburst and also to accurately constrain the geometry of the inner accretion disk.

name: MAXI_J1543m564
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of the transient black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1543-564 coordinated with XRISM
abstract: MAXI J1543-564 is a transient black hole X-ray binary (BH XRB) candidate, with one previous outburst detected in 2011 (Stiele et al., 2012). The source was detected in outburst by MAXI in Dec. 2025, and observed with NuSTAR on 26-12-2025. This observation showed the source was in its intermediate state, with strong reflection features and a narrow absorption line at ~6.9 keV. The presence of this absorption feature has been confirmed with blind searches, and an absorption line included in phenomenological model fits significantly improves the fit statistics. The source has since transitioned into the soft state (confirmed by Swift/XRT monitoring) and has remained at ~30 mCrab (still detected in MAXI light curves). Given this transition, and the fact that disk wind features are more prominent in soft-state spectra, it's very likely that the absorption line feature will still be present. Given the presence of this absorption line, a XRISM DDT observation has just been approved, and is scheduled to begin on 2026-01-28. XRISM has not yet detected a disk wind feature in any BH XRB, and the planned observation may be the first opportunity to leverage XRISM's remarkable spectral resolution to study this behavior. XRISM's relatively narrow bandpass, and the fact that the detected absorption line falls directly in the broad Fe K alpha emission region makes analysis of the expected XRISM data extremely complex. To resolve this, broadband constraints of the source continuum, and in particular constraints on the reflection spectrum around 7 keV and above 10 keV, will prove invaluable. Only NuSTAR is capable of constraining the broadband emission, whether that continuum emission is simple or in the case that it includes signatures of relativistic reflection. This requested NuSTAR DDT will remove any ambiguity in analyzing the discrete spectral features detectable by XRISM, while simultaneously providing the first ever NuSTAR observation of MAXI J1543-564 in its soft state.

name: Cyg_X2
title: NuSTAR calibration campaign
abstract: Observations of celestial sources will be undertaken throughout the mission to determine, and then monitor changes to, the calibration of the X-ray observatory. Observations will enable the calibration of absolute flux, spectral sensitivity, point spread function, and the timing capabilities of the observatory as well as the observatory optical alignment. NuSTAR will also participate in cross-calibration campaigns with the Chandra, XMM-Newton, Swift, and Suzaku X-ray observatories.

name: ARK564
title: X-RAY POLARIMETRY OF THE HIGHLY ACCRETING SEYFERT ARK 564
abstract: We propose an IXPE and NuSTAR observation of the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Ark 564, one of the X-ray brightest high accretion rate AGN. IXPE observations of moderately accreting Seyferts to date point to radially extended slab or wedge-like coronae, yet the high-Eddington regime is still unexplored. A 2 Ms IXPE exposure of Ark 564 will allow polarization to be measured at a few percent level (MDP ~ 2.5%), sufficient to discriminate between competing models for the Comptonizing medium geometry. A simultaneous NuSTAR 100 ks exposure will provide independent constraints on the coronal temperature and the reflection component, ensuring a physically self-consistent interpretation. This campaign will deliver the first robust measurement of X-ray polarization in a highly accreting Seyfert.

name: GS_1354m64
title: THE FIRST SAMPLE OF JET PROPERTIES FROM BLACK HOLES AND NEUTRON STARS
abstract: Astrophysical jets are powerful streams of gas and energy that form when matter falls onto compact objects with extreme gravity, which have a huge impact on their nearby environment. However, there are still key open questions regarding jets are launched or powered. Fast optical/infrared and X-ray variability studies of black hole and neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) recently opened a new way to constrain the base of the jet, discovering a new rich and exciting phenomenology. An XMM-Newton+VLT proposal has been recently awarded to observe with weekly cadence any LMXB which shows a jet with simultaneous X-ray/IR high time resolution observations. Here we propose to match this program with 8 NuSTAR+NICER observations, in order to obtain high quality spectral timing measurements.
subject_category: Proposed ToOs and Directors Discretionary Time

name: WISSH_57
title: A NUSTAR WISSHFUL PROGRAM: X-RAY CORONAE AND WINDS IN QUASARS AT COSMIC NOON
abstract: We propose coordinated NuSTAR observations (880ks in total) of four luminous, high-redshift quasars (z ~ 2) from the XMM WISSHFUL program - among the most luminous and rapidly accreting known - to systematically study coronal properties and their connection to nuclear winds. By leveraging such deep XMM and NuSTAR observations, we will precisely measure high-energy cut-offs, which is crucial for understanding pair-production mechanisms and potential non-thermal coronae and constrain the continuum close to the UFO absorption features, which is critical to determine their significance and properties, and to investigate the link between the nuclear winds and accretion properties in an almost unexplored regime of redshift, luminosity and accretion rate.

name: GS_1354m64
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GS 1354-64
abstract: GS~1354-64, probably the farthest black hole known in the Milky Way, was discovered in February 1987 when it went into an outburst and was observed by Ginger. The source underwent additional outbursts in November 1997 and in June 2015---the 1997 outburst holds the record for the largest total energy radiated during an outburst in known-distance galactic black hole X-ray novae. Also, unlike the 1987 outburst, the source remained in a hard state throughout both the 1997 and the 2015 outbursts, making them plausibly the most luminous hard state observed in a black hole X-ray binary. The onset of a new outburst from the source was reported by MAXI on December 25, 2025 and the source flux has been rising steadily since. Thus, although no outburst was reported for GS 1354-64 around 2006/2007, it is highly likely that the source exhibits outbursts at intervals of 8-10 years. Spectroscopic studies of the companion, BW Cir, suggest it is an evolved G subgiant that has filled its Roche lobe and its luminosity puts the system at a distance of at least 27kpc. The enigmatic nature of this system, its clock-work outburst cycles, and its preference for hard-state only evolution makes it an ideal candidate for NuSTAR observations. While the source was observed a few times during the 2015 outburst, for a unique system like this, observing it again in the current outburst cycle will be crucial to probing how the system evolves in spectral/timing properties from outburst to outburst. Studying this source can potential provide insight into the origin of failed outbursts and how it relates to the accretion-flow disk instability model.

name: 1A_1118m61
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of 1A 1118-61
abstract: Swift/BAT has observed an X-ray brightening from the Be/X-ray binary 1A 1118-61 since 2025-01-17 (MJD 61057; ATel 17608). The 15-50 keV flux reached 1.6 Crab on 2025-01-18. Assuming the hard outburst spectrum reported during the 2009 giant outburst (NH = 0.8x10^22 cm^-2, # = 0.4; Maitra et al. 2012), WebPIMMS gives a 2-8 keV flux of 9x10^-9 erg s^-1 cm^-2, corresponding to a 2-8 keV luminosity of ~1x10^37 erg s^-1 at a distance of ~3 kpc. The system hosts a slowly rotating neutron star with Pspin # 406 s (Coe et al. 1994). This is the highest flux recorded for the source and strongly suggests the onset of a giant (Type II) outburst. A broad CRSF at ~50 keV (Maitra et al. 2012) implies a high magnetic field of ~6x10^12 G and suggests that the source is approaching the transition to the supercritical accretion regime. Pulse-phase-resolved spectroscopy revealed strong CRSF variability, indicating pronounced geometrical effects and/or a complex magnetic-field structure (Maitra et al. 2012). NuSTAR can uniquely address how the accretion-column geometry and radiative regime evolve as the source approaches the critical luminosity. With its high sensitivity and broad bandpass, NuSTAR will (i) measure the hard X-ray continuum and cutoff (ii) resolve and characterize the ~50 keV CRSF (centroid, width, depth) and search for luminosity- and phase-dependent shifts expected from changes in the line-forming region, and (iii) perform pulse-phase-resolved spectroscopy to connect spectral/CRSF variability directly to beam pattern. Finally, an additional science case is an extended monitoring of the QPO. 1A 1118-61 has previously shown QPOs around 0.07-0.09 Hz during a giant outburst (Maitra et al. 2012), with indications of energy-dependent QPO amplitude. We could (i) confirm whether QPOs reappear (ii) track how the QPO frequency rms evolve with luminosity across the regime transition. SRG/ART-XC observations in the 4-25 keV band are scheduled for 19 January 2025.

name: NGC628_ULX_1
title: BROADBAND X-RAY PROBE OF THE ULTRALUMINOUS SOURCE NGC 628 ULX-1
abstract: NGC 628 ULX-1 is a uniquely variable ultraluminous X-ray source exhibiting low-frequency QPOs that hint at super-Eddington accretion onto a compact object of ambiguous nature. We propose simultaneous NuSTAR and XMM-Newton observations to search for pulsations, precisely characterize QPOs, and constrain the accretion geometry.

name: Cyg_X3
title: DDT observations of Cyg X-3
abstract: Cyg X-3 is a microquasar known for its bright, recurrent flares observed from radio to gamma-rays. Recently, LHAASO detected transient PeV gamma-ray emission at the highest photon energy ever detected from Galactic sources, suggesting Cyg X-3 may be one of the most energetic Galactic PeVatrons. Such flares are likely tied to relativistic plasmoids and particles in the jet. In early February 2025, Cyg X-3 entered an ultra-soft/radio-quenched state, following a hard phase that began in August 2024. Historically, these states precede major flares with peak radio fluxes up to ~20 Jy. The duration of the ultra-soft/radio state varied from several days to several months in the past. In addition to the continuous monitoring by RATAN-600 (radio), soft X-ray (MAXI), hard X-ray (Swift/BAT), GeV (Fermi-LAT) and TeV (LHAASO) bands, our collaboration is planning a major observation campaign to capture the transition phase to a major flare by VLBA, SMA, XRISM and Astri-Mini (TeV) telescopes. We request NuSTAR DDT observations for this rare opportunity to observe the quench-to-flare transition phase in coordination with other telescopes. NuSTAR's broadband X-ray data will be uniquely valuable for multi-wavelength SED modeling (from radio to TeV gamma-rays) and complement high-resolution Fe line spectroscopy (with XRISM DDT to be requested) by characterizing the continuum X-ray emission.

name: Mrk_421
title: NuSTAR DDT observations of Mrk 421 coordinated with VERITAS
abstract: We request daily 7ks NuSTAR observations of the TeV blazar Mrk 421 on 3 consecutive days before January 22, 2026. Triggered by a once-in-a-decade TeV gamma-ray flare at a flux of 4 times the Crab Nebula flux, we wish to measure the flux and spectral variability of Mrk 421 simultaneously in X-ray and gamma-ray bands with Swift, Fermi, and VERITAS observations. The 4-100 keV X-ray flux measured by SVOM reveals an unprecedented flare in the hard X-ray band from Mrk 421, peaking at more than 10 times the level of previous NuSTAR observations.

name: AT2019wey
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of AT2019wey coordinated with Swift
abstract: In May 2025 the black hole candidate AT2019wey started fading in optical, accompanied by X-ray spectral softening (Rout et al. 2025, ATel #17190). We have been continuously monitoring this declining phase with LCO (optical) and Swift (X-rays and UV) since then. This phase is characterized by a double-dipping "W"-shaped evolution in the optical wavebands. The X-rays also show a similar pattern, but with a delay of about two weeks (see Figure 1). Over the last month, the optical flux shows a steady rise with the magnitudes decreasing by about ~0.7 in all filters. The X-ray flux, on the other hand, shows an interesting behaviour by first rising after the second dip and then suddenly decaying in the last three observations. While AT2019wey is a known source, the present state evolution is unprecedented and could not have been predicted for a GO proposal. The anti-correlated optical/X-ray evolution is challenging to explain and can potentially constrain theoretical models. During this time, the X-ray spectra from Swift/XRT continue to harden with the photon index gradually decreasing over this period. The hydrogen column density (N_H) almost doubled, suggesting that the source might have entered an obscured state similar to GRS 1915+105 (see Figure 2). The nature and properties of any obscuring material, if present, remains unclear and high resolution hard X-ray observations from NuSTAR can provide vital information regarding the same. Obscuring material can potentially generate additional distant reflection features and multiple emission and absorption lines that can be constrained with NuSTAR (e.g., Miller et al. 2020, Ratheesh et al. 2021). The source may also prove to be an analog of GRS 1915+105 which remained in a bright phase for several years before returning to an obscured state. We have approved LCO and Swift/XRT observations of the source until 07 February 2026 and the NuSTAR observations are requested to be (quasi-)simultaneous with them.

name: NGC1194
title: DISSECTING THE TORUS: A GOLDEN SAMPLE OF HEAVILY OBSCURED AGN WITH MULTI-EPOCH NUSTAR AND XMM OBSERVATIONS
abstract: Studies of heavily obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) suggest that the torus that causes the obscuration is clumpy, rather than uniform. The line-of-sight column density (NHlos) of the obscuring material should vary over weeks to months, but such an evidence has been observed only in a few X-ray detected AGN, due to lack of large samples of heavily obscured AGN with multi-epoch observations, which are key to characterize the obscuring material surrounding accreting SMBHs. We propose for a joint NuSTAR-XMM monitoring of 3 nearby Compton thick AGN with small torus covering factor and NH_los significantly larger than the torus average NH. Through this monitoring, we expect to measure significant variability in NHlos, and obtain the most accurate picture of nuclear obscuration in low-z AGN.

name: NGC235A
title: Extragalactic Surveys
abstract: The baseline NuSTAR extragalactic survey is comprised of three components: one deg^2 of the COSMOS field (50ks per position), 0.3 deg^2 of the ECDFS (200ks per position), and a ~3 deg^2 shallow survey (5ks per position), achieved by targeting 100 Swift-BAT identified AGNs.  Models predict that NuSTAR will detect ~200 AGNs in the COSMOS+E-CDF-S surveys and ~19 Compton-thick AGNs. The shallow survey will deliver a sample of serendipitous detection of AGNs in the NuSTAR field of view.

name: GS_1354m64
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of GS 1354-64
abstract: GS~1354-64, probably the farthest black hole known in the Milky Way, was discovered in February 1987 when it went into an outburst and was observed by Ginger. The source underwent additional outbursts in November 1997 and in June 2015---the 1997 outburst holds the record for the largest total energy radiated during an outburst in known-distance galactic black hole X-ray novae. Also, unlike the 1987 outburst, the source remained in a hard state throughout both the 1997 and the 2015 outbursts, making them plausibly the most luminous hard state observed in a black hole X-ray binary. The onset of a new outburst from the source was reported by MAXI on December 25, 2025 and the source flux has been rising steadily since. Thus, although no outburst was reported for GS 1354-64 around 2006/2007, it is highly likely that the source exhibits outbursts at intervals of 8-10 years. Spectroscopic studies of the companion, BW Cir, suggest it is an evolved G subgiant that has filled its Roche lobe and its luminosity puts the system at a distance of at least 27kpc. The enigmatic nature of this system, its clock-work outburst cycles, and its preference for hard-state only evolution makes it an ideal candidate for NuSTAR observations. While the source was observed a few times during the 2015 outburst, for a unique system like this, observing it again in the current outburst cycle will be crucial to probing how the system evolves in spectral/timing properties from outburst to outburst. Studying this source can potential provide insight into the origin of failed outbursts and how it relates to the accretion-flow disk instability model.

name: ARK564
title: X-RAY POLARIMETRY OF THE HIGHLY ACCRETING SEYFERT ARK 564
abstract: We propose an IXPE and NuSTAR observation of the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Ark 564, one of the X-ray brightest high accretion rate AGN. IXPE observations of moderately accreting Seyferts to date point to radially extended slab or wedge-like coronae, yet the high-Eddington regime is still unexplored. A 2 Ms IXPE exposure of Ark 564 will allow polarization to be measured at a few percent level (MDP ~ 2.5%), sufficient to discriminate between competing models for the Comptonizing medium geometry. A simultaneous NuSTAR 100 ks exposure will provide independent constraints on the coronal temperature and the reflection component, ensuring a physically self-consistent interpretation. This campaign will deliver the first robust measurement of X-ray polarization in a highly accreting Seyfert.

name: ESO317m41
title: PROBING THE STRUCTURE OF AGN TORI WITH NUSTAR
abstract: Variability in line-of-sight column density (NH,los) is critical for understanding the structure of the obscuring material in AGN. While studies suggest a clumpy torus, variability constraints for obscured AGN remain sparse, with most limited to months-to-years timescales and obscured (NH=10^22-24 cm^-2) but non-Compton-thick (NH>10^24 cm^-2) sources. This pilot study proposes a NuSTAR large program (750 ks) to perform the first systematic search for short-term variability in five nearby (z<0.02) Compton-thick Seyfert 2 galaxies, which exhibit year-scale NH,los variability. By probing days-to-weeks timescales, we will determine whether obscuration changes arise from compact clouds near the SMBH or larger-scale structures, providing critical constraints on the geometry of the AGN tori.

name: UGC_530
title: UNVEILING NEW COMPTON-THICK AGN IN THE LOCAL UNIVERSE
abstract: Compton-thick AGN are believed to represent a significant fraction of the cosmic X-ray background, especially around 30 keV. However, there is a discrepancy in the fraction obtained from population synthesis models and the observed fraction, mainly due to the bias against detecting heavily obscured AGN. To address this, we have developed a volume-limited sample of AGN detected by BAT. We select two sources that have soft X-ray data indicative of a Compton-thick scenario. We propose to jointly observe the two sources with NuSTAR and XMM-Newton to confirm their Compton-thick nature and constrain torus properties with physically motivated torus models. Doing so will allow us to accurately measure the Compton-thick AGN fraction in the local Universe after accounting for selection effects.

name: ABELL_1689
title: HOT GAS, HYDROSTATIC MASS, AND INVERSE COMPTON CONSTRAINTS IN ABELL 1914 & ABELL 1689
abstract: The abundance of galaxy clusters is an important cosmological probe: however, hydrostatic masses are significantly below what's expected, hindering their usefulness for cosmology. We propose to observe the massive galaxy clusters Abell 1689 & Abell 1914 to characterize their hot gas, compare to previous measurements, estimate their hydrostatic masses and to search for inverse Compton emission associated with their radio halos, which will constrain their magnetic field strengths and inform possible non-thermal pressure support leading to underestimates of their mass. ICM measurements of these clusters from Chandra and XMM derived maps will also be investigated in light of the broader cross-calibration discrepancy between these observatories.
subject_category: Galaxy clusters and extragalactic diffuse objects

name: ESP39607
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of ESP39607 coordinated with XRISM and XMM-Newton
abstract: We request a NuSTAR DDT observation to coordinate with the already-approved XRISM pointing of ESP 39607 (PI Peca, PID 22171) scheduled for the week of 2026 January 5, and the associated XMM observation (PI Peca, PID 096085). The XMM observation is part of a separate proposal, but will be coordinated with XRISM on a best-effort basis, planned for January 5???7, as after this period XMM cannot observe the target. Because XRISM joint proposals were not available in Cycle 2, this multi-mission coordination could not have been proposed through the standard GO program. ESP 39607 is one of the very few AGN showing an ultra-fast inflow (UFI), previously detected in two NuSTAR epochs (May 2023 and August 2024) with consistent line energy (4.8 keV obs-frame) and an infalling velocity of 0.15-0.20c (Peca+25a). It is also the only obscured AGN exhibiting such a feature, making it uniquely valuable for probing non-standard accretion mechanisms (e.g., failed winds, magnetic feeding, and chaotic accretion). XRISM will provide the first eV-resolution view of the infalling Fe-K complex, but proper interpretation requires a precise broadband X-ray continuum, which only the combination of NuSTAR and XMM can supply.

name: WISSH_49
title: A NUSTAR WISSHFUL PROGRAM: X-RAY CORONAE AND WINDS IN QUASARS AT COSMIC NOON
abstract: We propose coordinated NuSTAR observations (880ks in total) of four luminous, high-redshift quasars (z ~ 2) from the XMM WISSHFUL program - among the most luminous and rapidly accreting known - to systematically study coronal properties and their connection to nuclear winds. By leveraging such deep XMM and NuSTAR observations, we will precisely measure high-energy cut-offs, which is crucial for understanding pair-production mechanisms and potential non-thermal coronae and constrain the continuum close to the UFO absorption features, which is critical to determine their significance and properties, and to investigate the link between the nuclear winds and accretion properties in an almost unexplored regime of redshift, luminosity and accretion rate.

name: V1025_CEN
title: BROADBAND X-RAY STUDY OF ACCRETION GEOMETRY AND INVESTIGATING COMPTON REFLECTION IN EVOLVED LLIPS
abstract: Broadband X-ray spectra of LLIPs consist of multitemperature thermal plasma component,its reflection from white dwarf & 6.4 keV Fe fluorescence emission line. We propose simultaneous NuSTAR-XMM observation of three evolved LLIPs, DW Cnc, V1025 Cen and CC Scl for the first time to precisely measure the shock temperature and unambiguously detect the reflection hump. For all the sources, we request 50 ks of NuSTAR (Total 150 ks) & 25 ks of XMM observation (Total 75 ks).

name: PSR_J1417m4402
title: NUSTAR OBSERVATIONS OF A TRANSITIONAL MILLISECOND PULSAR CANDIDATE
abstract: Spider binaries are a recently recognized class of millisecond pulsar systems that appear to be the evolutionary link between recycled pulsars and their low-mass X-ray binary progenitors. To date, only three such binaries have been observed to switch between clearly distinguishable accreting and disk-free rotation-powered pulsar states. We have recently identified a pronounced enhancement in gamma-ray luminosity of the transitional pulsar candidate PSR J1417-4402 that may be indicative of a transformation to an accreting state. We propose a set of three 30 ks NuSTAR monitoring observations to study the hard X-ray properties of this system as part of a broader multiwavelength campaign.

name: 1ES_1927p654
title: TRACKING THE UNUSUALLY COOL CORONA DURING A REAL-TIME JET LAUNCH IN AN AGN
abstract: 1ES~1927+654 is an enigmatic changing look active galaxy (CL-AGN) which has recently shown a nascent bi-polar radio jet on pc scales, evolving at a speed of 0.2c, a unique event of jet formation and evolution in real-time from an AGN. Contemporaneous to the jet formation, multiple snapshots of NuSTAR observations have detected a cool corona kT = 8 keV. These extraordinary discoveries reveal intimate connections between jet formation and the heating/cooling rates in the corona (connected by magnetic fields). Here we propose to monitor this interesting source bimonthly with NuSTAR for the next 1 year with 40 ks exposure per snapshot (=240ks total) to track the long-term changes in the coronal temperature and slope as the jet forms and evolves.

name: PSR_J2022p3842
title: ENERGETIC PULSARS WITH UNDER-LUMINOUS NEBULAE: DECIPHERING PULSAR EMISSION
abstract: Of the hundreds of rotation-powered pulsars with detected wind nebulae (PWNe), three highly energetic examples stand out by their extremely underluminous nebulae relative to their spin-down power Edot. These highly modulated pulsars (60-100%) display other unusual properties, including an anomalously flat spectrum (Gamma approx. 1) in the 2 10 keV band that steepens at higher energies. We propose a NuSTAR observation of PSR J2022+3842 the most energetic but least studied example. The extreme properties of this object and its radio nebula may provide new insight into the emission mechanism of pulsars and their interaction with the local environment.

name: Sombrero_galaxy
title: NUSTAR/NICER/EVENT HORIZON TELESCOPE STUDIES OF LOW LUMINOSITY AGNS: JETS AND ACCRETION
abstract: In the past four years, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has assembled the first images of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) buried in the centers of galaxies. The successful radio and multi-wavelength (MW) imaging of M87 and SgrA* has paved the way for a new sample of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) targets. NGC 4594 (Sombrero galaxy/M104), IC 1459, NGC 3998, and NGC 4261 are among the very few AGNs that can be imaged at < 50 gravitational radii resolution. For this reason, these AGNs are all prime targets for EHT observations in 2025. We propose to observe up to two of these four systems with NuSTAR and NICER to complement EHT s 2025 campaign and investigate these AGNs' accretion, emission, and jet launching processes.

name: M51_ULX7
title: A HIGH-ENERGY STUDY OF THE SPECTRAL-TIMING VARIABILITY OF M51 ULX-7
abstract: The discovery of pulsating ultraluminous X-ray sources (PULXs) has opened the door to studying super-Eddington accretion onto compact objects. The detection of mHz quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the PULX M51 ULX-7 has shown that one should not blindly use the QPO frequency as a mass proxy of the (P)ULX accretor. With the present proposal, we ask for one joint, simultaneous NuSTAR/XMM pointing of M51 ULX-7 to perform a detailed spectral-timing study over the whole 0.3-25 keV energy range. ULX-7's spin pulsations have not been detected since 2019: a new observation could help us study the long-term evolution of the accreting NS. Little is still known about the mechanism producing these mHz QPOs. This work would represent the first study of these QPOs at energies greater than 10 keV.

title: SPECTRAL VARIABILITY OF HESS~J0632+057 PRECEDING AND FOLLOWING ITS UNIQUELY SHARP LIGHTCURVE PEAK
abstract: We propose NuSTAR observations of the high-mass gamma-ray binary HESS J0632+057 during its X-ray peak, a two-week interval where the flux varies by a factor of 10. The cause of this abrupt change is unknown. We aim to obtain two high-quality spectra to investigate spectral slope variations, absorption column changes, investigate any timing features, and potential thermal emission and Fe line at 6.4 keV linked to the peak. This data will test emission models involving colliding winds, accretion in the propeller regime, and enhanced absorption near periastron from the Be star s decretion disk.

name: LSXPS_J201940d5p3644
title: UNVEILING THE NATURE OF NEWLY DETECTED MEV GALACTIC SOURCES
abstract: We propose to observe 3 new candidates MeV emitting Galactic sources with NuSTAR for a total of 210ks. These sources have been detected for the very first time in the 20-200 MeV range and reside in the Galactic plane (b<5 deg). However, the lack of good-quality X-ray data hampers the source classification (e.g. SNR, PSR, PWN), and the characterization of their spectral properties (spectral index, shape, and flux). The excellent sensitivity of NuSTAR will enable us to fully characterize the SED from 3 keV - 200 MeV. Composing a broadband SED of these objects will enable us to (i) determine the nature of these newly discovered sources: (ii) perform a detailed study of their SED and compute their energetics.

name: V395_CAR
title: THE PRECISE TEST OF THE WIND DRIVING MECHANISMS FOR LOW-MASS X-RAY BINARIES
abstract: The understanding of accretion disc winds in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) gives us a rich physical insight into the accretion process, leading us to investigate the physical origin of AGN feedback. These winds are typically observed as blue-shifted absorption lines but could be observed as emission lines when the direct X-ray from the central source is blocked. The accretion disc corona (ADC) source shows those emission lines since the highly inclined disc blocks the direct photons. Those emission lines in the V395 Car are well described by the wind, which is driven by radiative heating and acceleration. Here, we propose a simultaneous NuSTAR observation with XRISM and NICER-IXPE for this object to conduct the most precise critical test of this wind-driving mechanism.

name: ARK564
title: X-RAY POLARIMETRY OF THE HIGHLY ACCRETING SEYFERT ARK 564
abstract: We propose an IXPE and NuSTAR observation of the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Ark 564, one of the X-ray brightest high accretion rate AGN. IXPE observations of moderately accreting Seyferts to date point to radially extended slab or wedge-like coronae, yet the high-Eddington regime is still unexplored. A 2 Ms IXPE exposure of Ark 564 will allow polarization to be measured at a few percent level (MDP ~ 2.5%), sufficient to discriminate between competing models for the Comptonizing medium geometry. A simultaneous NuSTAR 100 ks exposure will provide independent constraints on the coronal temperature and the reflection component, ensuring a physically self-consistent interpretation. This campaign will deliver the first robust measurement of X-ray polarization in a highly accreting Seyfert.

name: Gamma_Vel
title: EXPLORING THE DYNAMICS OF THE COLLIDING WIND REGION THROUGH KEY ORBITAL PHASE STUDIES OF GAMMA VEL
abstract: We request four NuSTAR observations of the colliding wind binary &#947:2 Vel at key orbital phases (0.04, 0.13, 0.59, 0.75) with a broad-aim of characterizing the (shock-heated) plasma in the wind-interaction zone. Two of these observations (at0.04 and 0.13) will coincide with upcoming HETG observations (Oct 13-15 and Oct 18-23, 2025), facilitating a joint high-resolution and broadband spectral analysis of the system. We request the observation at phase 0.13 to be 40 ks. With nearly a day in elapsed time, this observation will provide critical insight into the X-ray maximum, as its precise phase is uncertain, but close to 0.13. The remaining observations will be 20 ks each and will offer essential insights regarding wind interactions in this massive binary.

name: PSR_J2022p3842
title: ENERGETIC PULSARS WITH UNDER-LUMINOUS NEBULAE: DECIPHERING PULSAR EMISSION
abstract: Of the hundreds of rotation-powered pulsars with detected wind nebulae (PWNe), three highly energetic examples stand out by their extremely underluminous nebulae relative to their spin-down power Edot. These highly modulated pulsars (60-100%) display other unusual properties, including an anomalously flat spectrum (Gamma approx. 1) in the 2 10 keV band that steepens at higher energies. We propose a NuSTAR observation of PSR J2022+3842 the most energetic but least studied example. The extreme properties of this object and its radio nebula may provide new insight into the emission mechanism of pulsars and their interaction with the local environment.

name: 3I_ATLAS_pos18
title: NuSTAR DDT observation of comet 3I ATLAS (C/2025 N1) coordinated with XMM-Newton
abstract: Comets can emit up to 1 GW of soft X-rays (<2 keV) through solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) with neutral gases in their atmospheres (Bodewits et al. 2007). Since the discovery of this mechanism, an additional X-ray source has been proposed: the scattering and reflection of solar X-rays by attogram-sized dust grains in cometary comae. This process is one of the leading explanations for unidentified line emissions between 1-2 keV (Snios et al. 2018), which are otherwise difficult to reconcile with the freeze-in temperatures of solar-wind ions. Further evidence for dust grains too small to be detected at optical wavelengths comes from collimated CN jets observed in many comets that show no correlation with visible dust structures (A'Hearn et al. 1995), and from the narrow, sunward-facing jet observed by Deep Space 1 at 19P/Borrelly (Farnham et al. 2009), which was explained by the presence of `tiny' sub-micron-sized grains. We request 40 ks of NuSTAR DDT observations to search for high-energy X-ray emission from 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar comet discovered in our solar system. The coma of 3I/ATLAS likely harbors a significant population of very small dust grains, as indicated by a narrow, sunward jet similar to that of 19P/Borrelly (Farnham et al. 2009). Such features are thought to originate from tiny, volatile-rich grains, consistent with extended gas sources recently detected by JWST and Swift (Cordiner et al. 2025; Xing et al. 2025). Because the solar wind does not contain ions capable of producing X-ray emission above 2 keV, a NuSTAR detection of 3I/ATLAS would provide compelling evidence for X-ray reflectance by attogram-sized dust grains, establishing this as a new and diagnostically powerful emission process in cometary atmospheres. Such a detection would have broad implications for our understanding of dust-gas coupling, energy transport, and particle size distributions in both interstellar and solar-system comets.
